What you will be able to do after this page
  1. Explain why Wp​(α,β)=(minπ​∫dpdπ)1/p is a distance between probability measures, and redo the gluing proof of the triangle inequality (with matrices, then with random variables).
  2. Compare Wp​ and Wq​ on a compact space, and explain why they have the same convergent sequences without being “equivalent”.
  3. Tell apart weak, weak-*, vague and strong (total variation) convergence, and say which one Wp​ measures — on three test sequences: a moving Dirac, Riemann sums, and mass escaping to infinity.
  4. Prove Wpp​=21​∥α−β∥TV​ for the 0/1 distance, and the comparison W1​ versus total variation on a finite space (the two exercises of the sheet).
  5. Build the displacement interpolation αt​, prove it is a constant-speed geodesic, and explain why the mixture (1−t)α+tβ is not one.
  6. Define Wasserstein barycenters, compute them for Diracs, Gaussians and measures on the line, write the fixed-grid linear program, and run (and justify) the fixed-point algorithm.

The story of the lecture in five steps#

A transport cost between two distributions becomes a distance; a distance gives a notion of convergence and a geometry; in that geometry one can draw shortest paths and compute averages of distributions.

  1. Recap (§1). Kantorovich’s problem gives a number Lc​(α,β): the cost of the cheapest way to move the mass of α onto β when moving a unit of mass from x to y costs c(x,y).
  2. A distance (§2–§3). If the cost is a distance raised to a power, c=dp with p≥1, then Wp​=Lc1/p​ is a distance between probability measures. The key tool is the gluing of two transport plans. Different p give comparable distances.
  3. Convergence (§4–§5). What does “αn​→α” mean for distributions? Wp​-convergence is weak convergence (plus moments when the space is not compact). Total variation (the “strong” notion) is much stricter: it does not see how far mass moves, only whether it moves.
  4. Shortest paths (§6). Moving each unit of mass along a straight line, at constant speed, gives the displacement interpolation αt​. It is a shortest path (a geodesic) for W2​; fading one distribution into the other is not.
  5. Averages (§7–§9). The weighted average of points minimizes a sum of squared distances. Replace points by distributions and distances by W2​: you get Wasserstein barycenters. Closed forms for Diracs, Gaussians and 1D measures; a linear program on a grid; and a fixed-point algorithm in general.

What you need from Lessons 1 and 2#

Open only the refreshers you need. Each one says exactly what is used on this page.

Refresher — probability measures, Diracs, integrals

In this course, a probability measure α on a space X (a subset of Rd, a compact set, a finite set…) distributes a total mass 1 over X: α(A)≥0 is the mass of the set A, and α(X)=1. The set of all of them is written M1+​(X) in the lecture (“positive measures of mass 1”). Three kinds appear all the time:

  • A Dirac δx​: all the mass sits at the single point x. Then ∫fdδx​=f(x).
  • A discrete measure α=∑i​ai​δxi​​ with weights ai​≥0, ∑i​ai​=1 (a histogram): mass ai​ at the point xi​. Then ∫fdα=∑i​ai​f(xi​).
  • A measure with a density α=ρ(x)dx: then α(A)=∫A​ρ and ∫fdα=∫f(x)ρ(x)dx. Example: the uniform law U[0,1], density 1 on [0,1].

Probabilistic reading: “X∼α” means that the random variable X has law α, i.e. P(X∈A)=α(A); then E[f(X)]=∫fdα.

Refresher — push-forward T#​α

If T:X→Y is a map, the push-forward (image measure) T#​α is the measure obtained by moving each bit of mass of α from x to T(x):

(T#​α)(B)=α(T−1(B)),∫gd(T#​α)=∫g(T(x))dα(x).

Random variables: if X∼α then T(X)∼T#​α. Discrete: T#​(∑i​ai​δxi​​)=∑i​ai​δT(xi​)​ (the weights travel with their points). Used here for the marginals of a coupling (P1​(x,y)=x), for the displacement interpolation (Pt​(x,y)=(1−t)x+ty) and for the barycenter algorithm (T#​α with an averaged map T).

Refresher — couplings, and why an optimal one exists

A coupling (transport plan) of α and β is a probability measure π on pairs (x,y) whose two marginals are α and β. For histograms a∈Rn, b∈Rm it is a matrix P∈R+n×m​ with

j∑​Pij​=ai​  (row sums),i∑​Pij​=bj​  (column sums).

Pij​ is the mass sent from xi​ to yj​. There is always at least one coupling, the independent one Pij​=ai​bj​ (the product measure α⊗β), so the set of couplings is never empty. The minimum of ∫cdπ over couplings is attained (general Kantorovich problem, Lesson 2) (for a continuous cost on a compact space, and more generally for lower semi-continuous costs on Polish spaces such as Rd): there is an optimal coupling. Used here in the proof that Wp​(α,β)=0 forces α=β, and every time we write “let π be an optimal plan”.

Refresher — optimal transport on the line (CDF and quantiles)

For a probability α on R, the cumulative distribution function is Cα​(x)=α((−∞,x]) and the quantile function is its generalized inverse Cα−1​(t)=inf{x: Cα​(x)≥t}, t∈(0,1). The quantile function is non-decreasing; Cα−1​(t) is “the point below which a fraction t of the mass lies”.

On the line, the optimal plan for ∣x−y∣p with p≥1 is the monotone one (sorted mass goes to sorted mass: the t-th quantile of α goes to the t-th quantile of β), and

Wpp​(α,β)=∫01​​Cα−1​(t)−Cβ−1​(t)​pdt.

When α has a density, the monotone plan is the map T=Cβ−1​∘Cα​. Used here for every 1D computation (Riemann sums, Gaussians on the line, 1D barycenters).

Refresher — Brenier’s theorem and Gaussians (Lesson 1)

Brenier. On Rd with c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2: if α has a density, there is a unique optimal plan, and it is carried by the graph of a map T=∇φ with φ convex: π=(Id,T)#​α, i.e. Y=T(X). Conversely, the gradient of any convex function is the optimal map between α and (∇φ)#​α. So Kantorovich (plans) and Monge (maps) give the same answer.

Gaussians. Between N(mα​,Σα​) and N(mβ​,Σβ​) the optimal map is affine, T(x)=mβ​+A(x−mα​) with the symmetric positive matrix

A=Σα−1/2​(Σα1/2​Σβ​Σα1/2​)1/2Σα−1/2​,

and W22​=∥mα​−mβ​∥2+B(Σα​,Σβ​)2 with the Bures distance B(Σ,Λ)2=tr(Σ+Λ−2(Λ1/2ΣΛ1/2)1/2). In 1D: T(x)=mβ​+σα​σβ​​(x−mα​) and W22​=(mα​−mβ​)2+(σα​−σβ​)2. Here M1/2 is the matrix square root: diagonalize M=UDU⊤ (with D≥0) and set M1/2=UD1/2U⊤. Used here in §6 (geodesics) and §8–§9 (barycenters).

1. Recap: the Kantorovich problem notes p. 1#

Choose how the random pair (X,Y) is dependent, keeping the laws of X and Y fixed, so that the average cost E[c(X,Y)] is as small as possible.

On the board notes p. 1, top

α,β∈M1+​(X)×M1+​(Y),

U(α,β)={π∈M1+​(X×Y) ; P1​#​π=α,  P2​#​π=β},P1​(x,y)=x,P2​(x,y)=y.

Kantorovich formulation of OT (c = cost function):

Lc​(α,β)=π∈U(α,β)inf​∫X×Y​c(x,y)dπ(x,y)=X∼α, Y∼βinf​E[c(X,Y)].

Brenier: on Rd, c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2 → equivalence with Monge.

Decoding the board#

π∈M1+​(X×Y)
A probability measure on pairs (x,y). Read π(A×B) as “the mass that starts in A and ends in B”.
P1​#​π=α
“The first marginal of π is α”: forgetting where the mass goes, you recover where it comes from. Explicitly π(A×Y)=α(A) for every set A. For matrices: the row sums of P are a.
P2​#​π=β
“The second marginal is β”: π(X×B)=β(B). For matrices: the column sums of P are b.
∫cdπ
The total cost of the plan: each unit of mass going from x to y pays c(x,y). For matrices: ∑i,j​Pij​c(xi​,yj​)=⟨P,C⟩.
infX∼α,Y∼β​E[c(X,Y)]
The same problem in the language of random variables. A coupling is the joint law of a random pair (X,Y) whose individual laws are prescribed. The laws of X and of Y are fixed; what you choose is how X and Y depend on each other.
Worked example — all the couplings of a tiny problem

Take α=β=21​δ0​+21​δ1​ (a fair coin, twice) and c(x,y)=∣x−y∣2. A coupling is a 2×2 matrix with row sums and column sums 21​:

Ps​=(s21​−s​21​−ss​),0≤s≤21​.

Its cost is ∑ij​(Ps​)ij​∣xi​−yj​∣2=2(21​−s)=1−2s (only the off-diagonal entries move mass, by a distance 1).

  • s=41​: the independent coupling (X and Y two independent coins). Cost 21​.
  • s=0: Y=1−X (anti-correlated coins). Cost 1, the worst.
  • s=21​: Y=X (the same coin read twice). Cost 0, the best.

So Lc​(α,α)=0, reached by the coupling “Y=X”. Keep this in mind: it is exactly the argument of §2 that Wp​(α,α)=0.

Brenier, in one sentence (why it was recalled)

On Rd with c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2, if α has a density, the optimal coupling does not split mass: it is π=(Id,T)#​α with T=∇φ, φ convex (“Y=T(X)”). So the relaxed problem of Kantorovich has the same solution as the problem of Monge. It was recalled at the start because the second half of the lecture uses maps: the displacement interpolation is built from T (§6), and the barycenter algorithm averages maps Tk​ (§9). See the refresher.

Fine print: “inf” is in fact “min”

The board writes inf. The infimum is attained: this was seen with the general Kantorovich problem (Lesson 2; in the first companion, Lesson 2 §6), because the set of couplings is compact for weak convergence and the cost is continuous or lower semi-continuous. We will use this in §2: “let π be an optimal plan”.

What is U(δx​,δy​), and what is Lc​(δx​,δy​)?

Answer

All the mass starts at x and all of it must arrive at y, so there is a single coupling, π=δ(x,y)​ (the pair (X,Y) is the constant (x,y)). Hence Lc​(δx​,δy​)=c(x,y). Diracs are the simplest test case of every statement of this page.

What is U(α,δy​) for an arbitrary α?

Answer

Every unit of mass must go to y: the only coupling is α⊗δy​ (the pair (X,y) with X∼α). Hence Lc​(α,δy​)=∫c(x,y)dα(x). We use this in §7 to find the barycenter of Diracs.

2. Wp​ is a distance notes p. 1–2#

Raise a ground distance to a power p≥1, solve the transport problem, take the p-th root: the result is a distance between probability measures, and its triangle inequality comes from “gluing” two transport plans end to end.

Why we want a distance#

Kantorovich gives a number Lc​(α,β) to every pair of distributions. To do more than compare two distributions once — to say that a sequence of distributions converges, to draw the shortest path between two of them, to average several of them — we need this number to behave like a distance. Two observations show that this is not automatic, and what the right construction is.

  • Not every cost works. Take c(x,y)=∣x−y∣2 on R and three Diracs. Then Lc​(δ0​,δ2​)=4, but Lc​(δ0​,δ1​)+Lc​(δ1​,δ2​)=1+1=2: going directly is more expensive than stopping half-way, so the triangle inequality fails.
  • Usual distances between densities are blind to geometry. ∥ρα​−ρβ​∥L2​ is not defined for Diracs, and it gives the same value to two bumps that do not overlap, whether they are 1 or 1000 apart. A transport distance sees how far the mass has to travel: we will see that Wp​(δx​,δy​)=d(x,y).

The fix found in class: start from a genuine distance d, use the cost c=dp with p≥1, and take the p-th root at the end. For the example above, W2​(δ0​,δ2​)=4​=2≤W2​(δ0​,δ1​)+W2​(δ1​,δ2​)=1+1.

The statement#

On the board notes p. 1

Metric properties. Proposition (p≥1). Assume X=Y is a metric space with a distance d, i.e.

d(x,y)=d(y,x)≥0,d(x,y)=0⟺x=y,d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z).

For 2 measures α,β∈M1+​(X) define

Wp​(α,β)=Ldp​(α,β)1/p=(π∈U(α,β)inf​∫dp(x,y)dπ)1/p.

Then Wp​ is a distance, called the p-Wasserstein distance.

Decoding

metric space (X,d)
A set with a distance. The three conditions are: symmetry and positivity; definiteness (distance zero only between a point and itself); triangle inequality (a detour through y never shortens the trip from x to z). Examples: Rd with ∥x−y∥; a finite set with any distance matrix; a sphere with the arc length.
p≥1
Written in red on the board: the proof of the triangle inequality uses Minkowski’s inequality, which is false for p<1 (see below).
Ldp​
The Kantorovich cost of §1 with c(x,y)=d(x,y)p.
(⋯)1/p
The p-th root. It is not decoration: it is what makes the triangle inequality true (example above).
“Wp​ is a distance”
The same three properties as d, but for distributions: Wp​(α,β)=Wp​(β,α)≥0; Wp​(α,β)=0⟺α=β; Wp​(α,γ)≤Wp​(α,β)+Wp​(β,γ).
Where Wp​ is finite

On a compact X (bounded), dp is bounded, so Wp​<∞ for all probability measures: this is the setting of the board, M1+​(X). On Rd one restricts to Pp​(Rd), the measures with ∫∥x∥pdα<∞; then the independent coupling already has a finite cost, because ∥x−y∥p≤2p−1(∥x∥p+∥y∥p). The metric space (Pp​(Rd),Wp​) is called the Wasserstein space.

First computations
  • Two Diracs. The only coupling is δ(x,y)​ (§1), so Wp​(δx​,δy​)=(d(x,y)p)1/p=d(x,y) for every p. The ground space sits inside the Wasserstein space without distortion: x↦δx​ preserves distances.
  • A small amount of mass moved. On R, let α=δ0​ and β=(1−ε)δ0​+εδ1​. The only coupling of δ0​ with β sends mass 1−ε from 0 to 0 (cost 0) and mass ε from 0 to 1 (cost 1p). So Wp​(α,β)=ε1/p: W1​=ε but W2​=ε​. Remember this pair: it shows in §3 that W1​ and W2​ can be very different numbers.

Symmetry, positivity, and “Wp​=0 only if α=β”#

On the board notes p. 1

Proof: symmetry, + positiveness derive from sym and posi of d.

Wp​(α,β)=0 ​⇒ ∃ coupling (X,Y) of π s.t. E(∥X−Y∥p)=0 ⇒ X=Y a.s.⇒ X and Y have the same distribution ⇒ α=β.​

Positivity. dp≥0, so every ∫dpdπ is ≥0, and so is their infimum.

Symmetry. Flip each pair: the map s(x,y)=(y,x) turns a coupling π of (α,β) into a coupling s#​π of (β,α), and back. It does not change the cost, because d(y,x)=d(x,y). So the two infima are taken over the same set of numbers. (For matrices: write Dij​=d(xi​,yj​), an n×m matrix. Then P∈U(a,b)⟺P⊤∈U(b,a); the reversed problem, from β to α, has cost matrix (d(yj​,xi​)p)ji​=(Dp)⊤ because d is symmetric; and ⟨P⊤,(Dp)⊤⟩=⟨P,Dp⟩.)

Definiteness. One direction is the worked example of §1: if α=β, take X∼α and Y=X; this coupling costs E[d(X,X)p]=0, so Wp​(α,α)=0. The other direction is the chain on the board:

  1. Assume Wp​(α,β)=0 and let π be an optimal coupling, so ∫dpdπ=0.An optimal coupling exists (Lesson 2). This is why the board can say “there exists a coupling with E=0”: without existence we would only have couplings with cost →0.
  2. Let (X,Y)∼π. Then E[d(X,Y)p]=0.This is the same integral, written with random variables.
  3. So d(X,Y)=0 almost surely, i.e. X=Y almost surely.A non-negative random variable with zero mean is zero almost surely; then definiteness of d.
  4. For every set A: α(A)=P(X∈A)=P(Y∈A)=β(A). Hence α=β.If two random variables are almost surely equal they have the same law; and X∼α, Y∼β by definition of a coupling.

The triangle inequality: the idea of “gluing”#

We want Wp​(α,γ)≤Wp​(α,β)+Wp​(β,γ). Since Wp​(α,γ) is a minimum over couplings of α and γ, it suffices to exhibit one coupling of α and γ whose cost is at most the right-hand side. The natural candidate: travel from α to β with an optimal plan, then from β to γ with another optimal plan. Two questions:

  • With maps it would be easy: if T#​α=β and S#​β=γ, then (S∘T)#​α=γ, and pointwise d(x,S(T(x)))≤d(x,T(x))+d(T(x),S(T(x))).
  • With plans the mass arriving at a middle point yj​ comes from several xi​, and the mass leaving yj​ goes to several zk​. We must decide which part of the arriving mass leaves for which destination. The simplest rule: don’t look at where it came from. Each bit of mass at yj​ leaves for zk​ in the proportion used by the second plan, πβγ​(j,k)/bj​.

That rule is the gluing. Probabilistically: build a triple (X,Y,Z) in which (X,Y) follows the first plan, (Y,Z) follows the second, and Z is chosen knowing only Y.

The discrete proof, step by step#

On the board notes p. 1, bottom

Triangle inequality. Let’s start with the discrete case:

α=i∑​ai​δxi​​,β=j∑​bj​δyj​​,γ=k∑​ck​δzk​​.

Write παβ​ and πβγ​ the optimal plans between α and β, and between β and γ. We construct a 3D tensor S by gluing these 2 plans:

[drawing: α παβ​ ​β πβγ​ ​γ]

Sijk​:=⎩⎨⎧​bj​παβ​(i,j)πβγ​(j,k)​0​if bj​=0,otherwise.​
i∑​Sijk​=πβγ​(j,k)​k∑​Sijk​=παβ​(i,j)⇒ the 3 marginals of S are (a,b,c).
On the board notes p. 2, top
Define  παγ​:=i,k∑​(j∑​Sijk​)δ(xi​,zk​)​∈U(α,γ).
Wp​(α,γ)​≤(i,k∑​παγ​(i,k)d(xi​,zk​)p)1/p≤(i,j,k∑​Sijk​(d(xi​,yj​)+d(yj​,zk​))p)1/p≤(ijk∑​Sijk​d(xi​,yj​)p)1/p+(ijk∑​Sijk​d(yj​,zk​)p)1/p≤Wp​(α,β)(ij∑​παβ​(i,j)d(xi​,yj​)p)1/p​​+Wp​(β,γ)(jk∑​πβγ​(j,k)d(yj​,zk​)p)1/p​​​

In red: ∥a∥p,S​:=(∑Sijk​aijkp​)1/p.

Decoding S: mass that travels along a path

Read Sijk​ as the mass that goes xi​→yj​→zk​. The formula is a product of two readable factors:

Sijk​=mass from xi​ arriving at yj​παβ​(i,j)​​×fraction of the mass at yj​ that leaves for zk​bj​πβγ​(j,k)​​​.

The second factor is a proportion: the plan πβγ​ sends a total bj​ out of yj​ (its row sums are b), of which πβγ​(j,k) goes to zk​. The rule applies the same proportions to the mass coming from every xi​ — the “don’t look where it came from” rule. When bj​=0, no mass passes through yj​, and Sijk​=0.

Step 1 — the three marginals of S

  1. k∑​Sijk​=bj​παβ​(i,j)​k∑​πβγ​(j,k)=bj​παβ​(i,j)​bj​=παβ​(i,j)(bj​=0).
    Row j of πβγ​ sums to bj​ (first marginal of πβγ​ is β). Interpretation: all the mass from xi​ arriving at yj​ leaves yj​ somewhere.
  2. If bj​=0, both sides are 0.Column j of παβ​ has non-negative entries summing to bj​=0, so παβ​(i,j)=0 for all i. (This is why dividing by bj​ is harmless.)
  3. i∑​Sijk​=bj​πβγ​(j,k)​i∑​παβ​(i,j)=bj​πβγ​(j,k)​bj​=πβγ​(j,k).
    Column j of παβ​ sums to bj​ (second marginal of παβ​ is β).
  4. j,k∑​Sijk​=j∑​παβ​(i,j)=ai​,i,k∑​Sijk​=bj​,i,j∑​Sijk​=j∑​πβγ​(j,k)=ck​.
    Sum the identities of lines 1–3 once more. So the three “one-index marginals” of S are a, b, c: S is a probability on triples (xi​,yj​,zk​) whose pair-marginals are the two plans.

Step 2 — a coupling of α and γ

Forget the middle point: παγ​(i,k)=∑j​Sijk​ is the mass that goes from xi​ to zk​ (through any yj​). Its row sums are ∑j,k​Sijk​=ai​ and its column sums are ∑i,j​Sijk​=ck​ (Step 1, line 4), so παγ​∈U(α,γ). In matrix form, παγ​=παβ​diag(1/b)πβγ​ (with 1/bj​ replaced by 0 when bj​=0).

Step 3 — the chain of inequalities, line by line

  1. Wp​(α,γ)≤(i,k∑​παγ​(i,k)d(xi​,zk​)p)1/p
    Wpp​ is the minimum of the cost over couplings, and παγ​ is one coupling (Step 2). Any coupling gives an upper bound.
  2. =(i,j,k∑​Sijk​d(xi​,zk​)p)1/p
    Replace παγ​(i,k) by its definition ∑j​Sijk​ (the summand does not depend on j).
  3. ≤(i,j,k∑​Sijk​(d(xi​,yj​)+d(yj​,zk​))p)1/p
    Triangle inequality of d: d(xi​,zk​)≤d(xi​,yj​)+d(yj​,zk​); and t↦tp is increasing on [0,∞); and Sijk​≥0.
  4. ≤(ijk∑​Sijk​d(xi​,yj​)p)1/p+(ijk∑​Sijk​d(yj​,zk​)p)1/p
    Minkowski’s inequality ∥u+v∥p,S​≤∥u∥p,S​+∥v∥p,S​ for the weighted norm written in red on the board, with uijk​=d(xi​,yj​) and vijk​=d(yj​,zk​). It needs p≥1 (refresher below).
  5. =(ij∑​παβ​(i,j)d(xi​,yj​)p)1/p+(jk∑​πβγ​(j,k)d(yj​,zk​)p)1/p
    In the first sum the summand does not depend on k: sum over k first and use ∑k​Sijk​=παβ​(i,j). In the second, sum over i first and use ∑i​Sijk​=πβγ​(j,k) (Step 1).
  6. =Wp​(α,β)+Wp​(β,γ).
    The plans παβ​ and πβγ​ were chosen optimal.
Refresher — Minkowski’s inequality, and why p≥1

Let wm​≥0 be weights (here m=(i,j,k) and w=S). For p≥1, the quantity ∥u∥p,w​=(∑m​wm​∣um​∣p)1/p is a (semi-)norm: it is the ℓp norm of the vector (wm1/p​um​)m​. In particular it satisfies the triangle inequality, which is Minkowski’s inequality:

(m∑​wm​∣um​+vm​∣p)1/p≤(m∑​wm​∣um​∣p)1/p+(m∑​wm​∣vm​∣p)1/p.

The same holds for random variables: E[∣U+V∣p]1/p≤E[∣U∣p]1/p+E[∣V∣p]1/p (the triangle inequality of the Lp norm). It is false for p<1: with p=21​, w=(1,1), u=(1,0), v=(0,1), the left side is (1+1)2=4 and the right side is 1+1=2. That is why the board writes p≥1 in red.

Worked example — gluing by hand

On the line, take

α=21​δ0​+21​δ2​,β=41​δ0​+21​δ1​+41​δ2​,γ=21​δ1​+21​δ3​.

On R the optimal plans are the monotone ones (refresher): fill the targets from left to right. That gives (rows = sources, columns = targets, ordered left to right)

παβ​=(41​0​41​41​​041​​),πβγ​=​41​41​0​041​41​​​.

The middle point y=1 receives 41​ from 0 and 41​ from 2 (total b=21​), and sends half of its mass to 1 and half to 3. The gluing splits each incoming bit in these proportions. The six paths that carry mass are:

path x→y→zπαβ​(i,j)×πβγ​(j,k)/bj​Sijk​
0→0→141​×1/41/4​41​
0→1→141​×1/21/4​81​
0→1→341​×1/21/4​81​
2→1→141​×1/21/4​81​
2→1→341​×1/21/4​81​
2→2→341​×1/41/4​41​

Summing over the middle point gives the glued plan παγ​=(3/81/8​1/83/8​) (rows x=0,2; columns z=1,3): row and column sums are 21​, as promised. With p=2 the chain of inequalities reads

W2​(α,γ)1​​ ≤ glued plan2​≈1.414​​ ≤ through y3​≈1.732​​ ≤ W2​(α,β)+W2​(β,γ)1/2​+3/2​≈0.707+1.225=1.932​​.

The first inequality is strict: the glued plan is admissible but not optimal (the optimal plan sends 0→1 and 2→3, cost 1). By forgetting where the mass came from, the gluing sends some mass from 0 to 3 and from 2 to 1. That is fine: the proof only needs an upper bound. The second inequality is strict because of the path 2→1→3, which goes back before going forward: d(2,3)=1<d(2,1)+d(1,3)=3 (on the five other paths the triangle inequality is an equality). The third one (Minkowski) is strict because the two vectors uijk​=d(xi​,yj​) and vijk​=d(yj​,zk​) are not proportional.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: the top row is α, the middle row β, the bottom row γ, each dot sized by its mass, at its position on the real line. The first panel draws the two optimal plans. Tap or hover a middle point: the paths through it light up, coloured by their starting point, and the readout shows the formula Sijk​=παβ​(i,j)πβγ​(j,k)/bj​ with its numbers. The second panel compares the glued plan παγ​ with the optimal plan. Change p or draw random histograms: the chain Wp​(α,γ)≤glued≤Wp​(α,β)+Wp​(β,γ) always holds.

The general case: gluing with random variables#

On the board notes p. 2

General case: triangle inequality. (α,β,γ): (X,Y) optimal for OT(α,β),

παβ​=P(X,Y)=PY​×PX∣Y​,πβγ​=P(Y~,Z)=PY~​×PZ∣Y~​,
παβγ​=PX∣Y​ PZ∣Y~​ PY​.
P(X,Y)
The joint law of the pair (X,Y); here it is the optimal plan παβ​.
PY​
The law of Y alone, i.e. β.
PX∣Y​
The conditional law of X given Y: “if you know that Y=y, where did this mass come from?”. In the discrete case, P(X=xi​∣Y=yj​)=παβ​(i,j)/bj​.
PY​×PX∣Y​
The chain rule: a joint law is “first draw Y, then draw X given Y”.
(Y~,Z)
A pair following the second optimal plan πβγ​. Since Y~ and Y both have law β, the gluing identifies them.
παβγ​
The glued law of a triple: draw Y∼β; then, given Y=y, draw X from PX∣Y=y​ and Z from PZ∣Y~=y​, independently of each other. “X and Z are conditionally independent given Y.”

In the discrete case this recipe gives back exactly S:  P(X=xi​,Y=yj​,Z=zk​)=bj​⋅bj​παβ​(i,j)​⋅bj​πβγ​(j,k)​=Sijk​. The general proof is then the discrete one, written with expectations:

  1. Wp​(α,γ)≤E[d(X,Z)p]1/p
    The law of (X,Z) is a coupling of α and γ: X∼α because (X,Y)∼παβ​, and Z∼γ because (Y,Z)∼πβγ​.
  2. ≤E[(d(X,Y)+d(Y,Z))p]1/p
    Triangle inequality of d, pointwise, and t↦tp increasing.
  3. ≤E[d(X,Y)p]1/p+E[d(Y,Z)p]1/p
    Minkowski’s inequality in Lp (the triangle inequality of the norm E[∣U∣p]1/p), valid for p≥1.
  4. =Wp​(α,β)+Wp​(β,γ).
    (X,Y) follows the optimal plan παβ​, and (Y,Z) follows the optimal plan πβγ​.
Fine print: the gluing lemma

For measures that are not discrete, the conditional laws PX∣Y=y​ must exist as a well-behaved family indexed by y (a “disintegration”). This is true on all the spaces of this course (Rd, compact metric spaces, and more generally Polish spaces). The statement “given two couplings with a common marginal, there is a law on triples with these two pair-marginals” is called the gluing lemma (Villani, Optimal transport, old and new, ch. 1).

Intuition — gluing is composition of plans

When both plans are maps, Y=T(X) and Z=S(Y), the conditional laws are Diracs and the glued triple is (X,T(X),S(T(X))): gluing is composition S∘T. For general plans it is the best one can do without remembering origins. The same trick proves the triangle inequality of many other transport distances.

Pitfall — forgetting the root, or taking p<1

W22​ is not a distance: W22​(δ0​,δ2​)=4>W22​(δ0​,δ1​)+W22​(δ1​,δ2​)=2. Always take the p-th root before using the triangle inequality. (For 0<p<1 the situation is reversed: dp is itself a distance, and it is Ldp​ without root that satisfies the triangle inequality.)

Pitfall — the glued plan is not the optimal plan

The glued plan παγ​ is only admissible. In the worked example it costs 2​ while W2​(α,γ)=1. Do not try to compute Wp​(α,γ) by gluing.

Reflexes
  • To prove an upper bound on Wp​(α,γ) → exhibit one coupling of α and γ and bound its cost.
  • To build a coupling of α and γ from couplings through β → glue: same middle point, conditionally independent ends.
  • To test any claim about Wp​ → try Diracs first: Wp​(δx​,δy​)=d(x,y).

Where exactly did the proof use p≥1, and where did it use that παβ​ and πβγ​ are optimal?

Answer

p≥1: only in Minkowski’s inequality (line 4 of the chain in Step 3, and line 3 of the general proof). Optimality: only in the very last line, to recognise Wp​(α,β) and Wp​(β,γ). With non-optimal plans you get Wp​(α,γ)≤(cost of παβ​)1/p+(cost of πβγ​)1/p, which is also true but weaker.

Compute Wp​((1−s)δ0​+sδ1​, (1−t)δ0​+tδ1​) on R for s≤t, and check the triangle inequality with a third value r in between.

Answer

The common mass stays in place; the excess t−s of the second measure at 1 must come from 0, at distance 1. So Wp​=(t−s)1/p. For s≤r≤t: (t−s)1/p≤(r−s)1/p+(t−r)1/p holds because u↦u1/p is concave and vanishes at 0, hence subadditive. For p=1 it is an equality.

3. Comparing Wp​ and Wq​ notes p. 2#

On a compact space, Wq​ is squeezed between Wp​ and a power of Wp​: all the Wasserstein distances agree on which sequences converge, even though their values can be very different.

The question#

We now have a whole family of distances W1​,W2​,W3​,… on the same set of distributions. Which one should we use? Do they at least agree on what “close” means? The answer of the lecture: on a compact space, yes for convergence, no for the numbers.

On the board notes p. 2

Topology of (M1+​(X),Wp​). Prop. Assume X compact. For 1≤p≤q we have

Wp​(α,β)≤Wq​(α,β)≤(diam(X))qq−p​Wp​(α,β)p/q,where diam(X)=x,ysup​d(x,y).

Proof: take φ(s)=sq/p; since q≥p, φ is convex on R+.

Wp​(α,β)q​≤(∫d(x,y)pdπ(x,y))q/pJensen≤​∫φ(d(x,y)p)dπ=∫d(x,y)qdπ=Wq​(α,β)qif π opt.​

[In the notes the powers q are missing on this line: it reads Wp​(α,β)≤(∫dpdπ)q/p, with Wq​(α,β) under the brace. They are restored here; the step-by-step proof below writes them carefully.]

d(x,y)q≤d(x,y)p≤diam(X)q−pd(x,y)q−p​​.

R.k: the notion of converging sequence is the same for all Wq​. R.k 2: all Wasserstein define the same topology (on a compact space).

Wp​(δx​,δy​)=d(x,y); if xn​→x in (X,d) then Wp​(δxn​​,δx​)→0 as n→+∞. [drawing: on a line, the point xn​ approaching x]

Decoding

diam(X)
The largest distance between two points of X. It is finite because X is compact (hence bounded). For X=[0,1], diam=1.
left inequality
“Wp​ increases with p.” Think of Wp​ as an average size of the displacements d(X,Y) under the best coupling: the Lp average gives more and more weight to the long displacements as p grows.
right inequality
“Wq​ is controlled by a power of Wp​.” Because no displacement can exceed diam(X), raising them to a higher power cannot make them explode.
“same topology”
A sequence αn​ converges to α for Wp​ if and only if it converges for Wq​. In a metric space, knowing the convergent sequences is knowing the topology (open sets, continuous functions…).
Refresher — Jensen’s inequality

If φ is convex and U is a random variable (or π a probability measure), then

φ(E[U])≤E[φ(U)],φ(∫fdπ)≤∫φ∘fdπ.

Picture: the graph of a convex function lies below its chords, so “the function of the average is below the average of the function”. With φ(s)=sr, r≥1, it says E[U]r≤E[Ur] for U≥0: this is the familiar fact that Lp norms on a probability space increase with p. Here we use r=q/p≥1.

The proof, step by step#

Idea of the proof
  1. Each inequality compares two transport costs; pick, for each, the coupling that makes one side exact (optimal for Wq​ on the left, optimal for Wp​ on the right).
  2. Left: compare the Lp and Lq averages of the displacement under the same coupling — Jensen.
  3. Right: bound dq by dp pointwise, using that d≤diam(X).
Proof of Wp​≤Wq​
  1. Let π be an optimal coupling for Wq​: ∫dqdπ=Wq​(α,β)q.“if π opt.” on the board: the coupling is optimal for the larger exponent q.
  2. Wp​(α,β)p≤∫d(x,y)pdπ(x,y).
    π is a coupling of α and β, maybe not optimal for dp, and Wpp​ is the minimum.
  3. Wp​(α,β)q≤(∫dpdπ)q/p=φ(∫dpdπ),φ(s)=sq/p.
    Raise step 2 to the power q/p; s↦sq/p is increasing on R+.
  4. φ(∫dpdπ)≤∫φ(dp)dπ=∫dqdπ.
    Jensen: φ is convex on R+ because q/p≥1, and π is a probability measure. Then φ(dp)=(dp)q/p=dq.
  5. Wp​(α,β)q≤Wq​(α,β)q,soWp​(α,β)≤Wq​(α,β).
    Step 1, then take the q-th root (increasing).

Note that compactness was not used here: Wp​≤Wq​ holds on any space (when both are finite).

Proof of Wq​≤diam(X)(q−p)/qWpp/q​
  1. Let π be an optimal coupling for Wp​ this time: ∫dpdπ=Wp​(α,β)p.Now we want an upper bound on Wq​, so we test Wq​ on the coupling that is good for Wp​.
  2. d(x,y)q=d(x,y)pd(x,y)q−p≤d(x,y)pdiam(X)q−pfor all x,y.
    d(x,y)≤diam(X) and q−p≥0, so dq−p≤diamq−p.
  3. Wq​(α,β)q≤∫dqdπ≤diam(X)q−p∫dpdπ=diam(X)q−pWp​(α,β)p.
    π is admissible for Wq​; integrate step 2; then step 1.
  4. Wq​(α,β)≤diam(X)qq−p​Wp​(α,β)qp​.
    Take the q-th root of both sides.
Note on the sources: your notes have the right exponent

The 2019 course notes (CourseOT.pdf, Proposition 8, p. 16) print the last factor as Wp​(α,β)q/p. The proof above gives Wpp/q​, as written in your notes. The example below confirms it: with q/p one would get W2​≤ε2, but in fact W2​=ε​.

The example that shows everything#

Worked example — moving a small mass ε by a distance 1

On X=[0,1] (so diam=1), take α=δ0​ and β=(1−ε)δ0​+εδ1​. We computed in §2 that Wp​(α,β)=ε1/p. So

W1​=ε,W2​=ε​,W4​=ε1/4.
  • Left inequality: ε≤ε​≤ε1/4 for ε∈[0,1]. ✓
  • Right inequality with (p,q)=(1,2): W2​≤11/2W11/2​=ε​. It is an equality: the bound cannot be improved.
  • Not equivalent: W2​/W1​=1/ε​→∞ as ε→0. There is no constant C with W2​≤CW1​ for all pairs. (Compare with norms in finite dimension, which are all equivalent up to constants.)
  • Same convergence: still, W1​→0 if and only if W2​→0 (both iff ε→0).
Intuition — what p measures

Moving a little mass far is cheap for W1​ (cost “mass × distance”) and expensive for large p (cost “(mass × distancep)1/p”, dominated by the distance). In the limit p→∞ one gets W∞​, the largest displacement needed, which does not care about the mass at all. So: W1​ for average displacement, large p when you care about the worst displacements.

Diracs: the topology of X is inside#

The last line of the board: since Wp​(δx​,δy​)=d(x,y), we have Wp​(δxn​​,δx​)→0 if and only if xn​→x. The map x↦δx​ sends the space X into the Wasserstein space without distortion; convergence of points is convergence of their Diracs. (This is the example that will separate Wp​ from the total variation in §5.)

Pitfall — “same topology” does not mean “same rates”

For αn​=(1−n1​)δ0​+n1​δ1​ and α=δ0​: W1​(αn​,α)=n1​ but W2​(αn​,α)=n​1​. Both converge, at different speeds. When a paper says “the error decays like n−1/2 in W2​”, the rate is tied to the choice of p.

Pitfall — compactness is needed for the right inequality

On R (not bounded), take αn​=(1−n1​)δ0​+n1​δn​​ and α=δ0​. Then W1​(αn​,α)=n1​n​=n​1​→0, but W2​(αn​,α)2=n1​(n​)2=1: W2​ does not converge. A vanishing mass travelling a growing distance is invisible to W1​ but not to W2​. We meet this phenomenon again in §4.

Reflexes
  • To compare two transport costs → use, for each side, the coupling that is optimal for the other side, and compare the integrands.
  • When you see a power sr with r≥1 and an average → think Jensen.
  • To show a bound is sharp, or that two distances are not equivalent → move a small mass ε by a fixed distance.

On X=[0,1], suppose W1​(αn​,α)≤n1​. What can you say about W3​(αn​,α)?

Answer

Right inequality with (p,q)=(1,3) and diam=1: W3​≤W11/3​≤n−1/3→0. Left inequality: W3​≥W1​, which gives nothing useful here. The rate n−1/3 is attained by the pair of the worked example with ε=n1​.

4. Convergence of measures, and what Wp​ measures notes p. 3#

Distributions are compared through test functions: αn​→α means ∫φdαn​→∫φdα for every φ in a class; on a compact space Wp​-convergence is exactly this “weak” convergence, and on Rd it is weak convergence plus convergence of the p-th moments.

The problem: what should “αn​→α” mean?#

For numbers or vectors there is one obvious notion of convergence. For distributions there are several, and the natural first guess is too strong. Asking αn​(A)→α(A) for every set A fails on the simplest example: δ1/n​ should converge to δ0​ (the point 1/n converges to 0), but with A={0}, δ1/n​(A)=0 for every n while δ0​(A)=1.

The way out is to look at distributions only through averages of nice functions: ∫φdαn​=E[φ(Xn​)]. Continuous test functions do not distinguish 1/n from 0 when n is large, which is what we want. The choice of the class of test functions gives the different notions.

On the board notes p. 3, top

Reminder of convergence of measures (for X not compact):

​(1)αn​weak​α(2)αn​weak*​α(3)αn​vague​α​​⟺∫φdαn​→∫φdα∀φ∈Cb​(X)⟺∫φdαn​→∫φdα∀φ∈C0​(X)⟺∫φdαn​→∫φdα∀φ∈Cc​(X)​

Prop: if (αn​) are probability measures and if α is a probability measure, then (1) ⟺ (2) ⟺ (3).

On a compact space X, Cb​(X)=C0​(X)=Cc​(X)=C(X).

Decoding the three classes of test functions

Take X=Rd to fix ideas. All three are classes of continuous functions; they differ by what happens far away.

Cb​(X)
bounded continuous functions: sup∣φ∣<∞. Examples: arctanx, cosx, the constant 1.
C0​(X)
continuous functions that tend to 0 at infinity: φ(x)→0 as ∥x∥→∞. Examples: e−x2, 1/(1+x2). Not the constant 1.
Cc​(X)
continuous functions with compact support: zero outside some bounded set. Example: the hat function max(0,1−∣x∣).

The names: “weak-*” because measures are the dual of C0​ (Riesz representation theorem), and convergence tested against the elements of the pre-dual is weak-* convergence in functional analysis. In probability, weak convergence is the familiar convergence in law: if Xn​∼αn​ and X∼α, then αn​→α weakly means E[φ(Xn​)]→E[φ(X)] for every bounded continuous φ (the central limit theorem is a statement of this kind).

Why the proposition needs “α is a probability measure”#

Worked example — a Dirac running away

On R, let αn​=δn​ (all the mass at the point n).

  • For φ∈C0​: ∫φdδn​=φ(n)→0. So δn​→0 weak-* and vaguely, where 0 is the zero measure!
  • For φ≡1∈Cb​: ∫1dδn​=1 for all n, while ∫1d0=0. So δn​→0 weakly. In fact δn​ has no weak limit at all: a weak limit would also be a vague limit, hence 0, which contradicts the test with φ≡1.

The mass has escaped to infinity: test functions that vanish at infinity cannot see it, the constant function can. The vague limit 0 is not a probability measure (it has lost its mass). The proposition says this is the only thing that can go wrong: if the limit keeps total mass 1, the three notions coincide.

Proposition (the board’s Prop, on X=Rd)

If αn​ and α are probability measures on Rd, then vague convergence implies weak convergence. Hence (1) ⟺ (2) ⟺ (3).

Idea of the proof

Weak ⇒ weak-* ⇒ vague is free (Cc​⊂C0​⊂Cb​). For the converse, cut a bounded test function into a compactly supported part, where vague convergence applies, and a part far away, where there is little mass — because α has mass 1 and so do the αn​, no mass can hide at infinity.

Full proof (vague ⇒ weak)

Fix φ∈Cb​ and ε>0.

  1. Choose R with α(BR​)≥1−ε, where BR​ is the ball of radius R.α(BR​)↑α(Rd)=1 as R→∞ (continuity of measures). Here we use that α has mass 1.
  2. Let χ(x)=min(1,max(0,R+1−∥x∥)): continuous, 0≤χ≤1, χ=1 on BR​, χ=0 outside BR+1​. So χ∈Cc​ and ∫χdα≥α(BR​)≥1−ε.A “cut-off” function.
  3. By vague convergence, ∫χdαn​→∫χdα≥1−ε, so ∫(1−χ)dαn​≤2ε for n large.∫(1−χ)dαn​=1−∫χdαn​ because αn​ has mass 1. Little mass of αn​ lies far away.
  4. Split φ=φχ+φ(1−χ):
    ​∫φdαn​−∫φdα​≤​∫φχdαn​−∫φχdα​+∥φ∥∞​∫(1−χ)dαn​+∥φ∥∞​∫(1−χ)dα.
    Triangle inequality, and ∣φ(1−χ)∣≤∥φ∥∞​(1−χ).
  5. The first term tends to 0 (vague convergence: φχ∈Cc​); the other two are at most 2ε∥φ∥∞​ and ε∥φ∥∞​ for n large. So limsupn​​∫φdαn​−∫φdα​≤3ε∥φ∥∞​ for every ε>0: the limit is 0.ε was arbitrary.
On a compact space there is only one notion

If X is compact, every continuous function is bounded (so C(X)=Cb​(X)), and its support is a closed subset of the compact X, hence compact (so C(X)=Cc​(X), and also =C0​(X): there is no “infinity” to escape to). The board’s line Cb​=C0​=Cc​=C(X) says: on a compact space we simply say weak convergence, αn​⇀α, meaning ∫φdαn​→∫φdα for every continuous φ.

Worked example — Diracs converge weakly exactly when the points converge

δxn​​⇀δx​ means φ(xn​)→φ(x) for every continuous bounded φ.

  • If xn​→x: true, by continuity of φ.
  • If xn​→x: there is r>0 with d(xn​,x)≥r for infinitely many n. The “bump” φ(y)=max(0,1−d(y,x)/r) is continuous and bounded, with φ(x)=1 but φ(xn​)=0 for those n. So no weak convergence.

Compare with the first guess “αn​(A)→α(A) for all A”, which rejected δ1/n​→δ0​: weak convergence accepts it. This is the convergence we want.

Wp​ metrizes weak convergence#

On the board notes p. 3

Prop: if X is compact, Wp​(αn​,α)n→+∞​0 if and only if αn​n→+∞​α. “Wp​ metrizes”.

Prop: if X is not compact,  Wp​(αn​,α)n→+∞​0⟺αn​n→+∞​α and ∫d(x,x0​)pdαn​n→+∞​∫d(x,x0​)pdα.

“Wp​ metrizes weak convergence”
Converging for the distance Wp​ is the same thing as converging weakly. So Wp​(αn​,α) is a number that tells you how far you are from the limit, for a notion of convergence (weak) that was defined without any number.
x0​
Any fixed reference point (for instance 0∈Rd); the condition does not depend on the choice.
∫d(x,x0​)pdα
The p-th moment of α: the average of the p-th power of the distance to x0​. For p=2 on Rd and x0​=0: E∥X∥2.

The compact case

Refresher — Lipschitz functions

A function f is L-Lipschitz if ∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤Ld(x,y) for all x,y: it cannot change faster than L times the distance travelled. The smallest such L is written Lip(f). On R: ∣x∣ and sinx are 1-Lipschitz; x2 is Lipschitz on every bounded interval but not on R (its slope is unbounded).

Idea of the proof
  1. Wp​→0⇒ weak. For a Lipschitz test function, ​∫fdαn​−∫fdα​≤Lip(f)W1​(αn​,α): move the mass with an optimal plan, and f changes by at most Lip(f) times the distance moved. Continuous functions are uniform limits of Lipschitz ones.
  2. Weak ⇒Wp​→0. Next lesson’s duality writes W1​ as a supremum of ∫fd(αn​−α) over 1-Lipschitz f; these f form a compact family, and weak convergence is uniform on compact families. Then §3 transfers the result from W1​ to Wp​.
Full proof of “Wp​→0⇒ weak”
  1. Let f be L-Lipschitz (∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤Ld(x,y)) and let πn​ be an optimal coupling for W1​(αn​,α). Then
    ∫fdαn​−∫fdα=∫(f(x)−f(y))dπn​(x,y).
    The marginals of πn​ are αn​ and α: ∫f(x)dπn​=∫fdαn​ and ∫f(y)dπn​=∫fdα.
  2. ​∫fdαn​−∫fdα​≤L∫d(x,y)dπn​=LW1​(αn​,α)≤LWp​(αn​,α).
    Lipschitz bound inside the integral; optimality of πn​; and W1​≤Wp​ (§3).
  3. Any continuous f on the compact X is a uniform limit of Lipschitz functions fk​ (lemma below). Then
    ​∫fd(αn​−α)​≤2∥f−fk​∥∞​+Lip(fk​)Wp​(αn​,α).
    Write f=fk​+(f−fk​); the second piece integrates to at most ∥f−fk​∥∞​ against each probability measure.
  4. Choose k to make the first term small, then n large to make the second small: ∫fdαn​→∫fdα.An “ε/2” argument.

Lemma (Lipschitz approximation). For continuous f on a compact metric space, fk​(x)=infy​(f(y)+kd(x,y)) is k-Lipschitz, fk​≤f, and fk​→f uniformly. Why: an infimum of k-Lipschitz functions of x is k-Lipschitz; y=x gives fk​≤f; and by uniform continuity, for ε>0 there is δ with ∣f(x)−f(y)∣<ε when d(x,y)<δ, while the points with d(x,y)≥δ give f(y)+kd(x,y)≥minf+kδ≥maxf≥f(x) once k≥(maxf−minf)/δ. So fk​(x)≥f(x)−ε.

Full proof of “weak ⇒Wp​→0” (uses Lesson 4)

We use the Kantorovich–Rubinstein formula, proved in the next lecture (duality): W1​(α,β)=sup{∫fd(α−β): f 1-Lipschitz}.

  1. Assume αn​⇀α but W1​(αn​,α)→0: along a subsequence, W1​(αn​,α)>ε, so there are 1-Lipschitz fn​ with ∫fn​d(αn​−α)>ε.Definition of a supremum.
  2. We may assume fn​(x0​)=0 for a fixed x0​.Subtracting a constant does not change ∫fn​d(αn​−α), because αn​−α has total mass 0.
  3. The functions fn​ are 1-Lipschitz and bounded by diam(X). By Arzelà–Ascoli, a further subsequence converges uniformly to some (1-Lipschitz) f.Equicontinuous and uniformly bounded functions on a compact space form a relatively compact family.
  4. ε<∫fn​d(αn​−α)≤∫fd(αn​−α)+2∥fn​−f∥∞​⟶0,
    a contradiction. So W1​(αn​,α)→0.Weak convergence for the fixed continuous f, and uniform convergence fn​→f.
  5. Wp​(αn​,α)≤diam(X)pp−1​W1​(αn​,α)p1​⟶0.
    The comparison of §3 with (p,q) replaced by (1,p). This is why the comparison of the Wp​ was proved just before: it reduces everything to W1​.

The non-compact case: mass escaping to infinity

On Rd the first half survives: Wp​→0 still implies weak convergence (bounded Lipschitz test functions are enough to characterise weak convergence). But weak convergence no longer implies Wp​→0. The obstruction is the one of the running Dirac, in a milder form: a vanishing amount of mass travelling an exploding distance.

Worked example — the escaping mass

On R, let αn​=(1−n1​)δ0​+n1​δn​ and α=δ0​.

  • Weak convergence holds: for bounded continuous φ, ∫φdαn​=(1−n1​)φ(0)+n1​φ(n)→φ(0), because ∣φ(n)∣/n≤∥φ∥∞​/n→0.
  • W1​ does not converge: the only coupling with δ0​ moves mass n1​ over a distance n, so W1​(αn​,α)=n1​⋅n=1 for every n. And W2​(αn​,α)=(n1​n2)1/2=n​→∞.
  • The moments do not converge: ∫∣x∣dαn​=n1​⋅n=1→0=∫∣x∣dα. The board’s condition fails, as it must.

Weak convergence does not see the small mass (it vanishes), transport does (it pays mass × distancep).

Why Wp​→0 forces the moments to converge (a one-line proof)

The p-th moment is itself a Wasserstein distance: the only coupling of α with δx0​​ sends everything to x0​, so ∫d(x,x0​)pdα=Wp​(α,δx0​​)p. The triangle inequality of Wp​ (§2) gives

​Wp​(αn​,δx0​​)−Wp​(α,δx0​​)​≤Wp​(αn​,α)⟶0,

so the moments converge. The converse direction of the board’s second proposition (weak convergence + moments ⇒Wp​→0) is harder: it uses Skorokhod’s representation and uniform integrability (Villani, Optimal transport, old and new, Theorem 6.9).

Reflexes
  • When you see “αn​→α” for distributions → ask “tested against which functions?”. On a compact space: continuous functions, and Wp​→0 is equivalent.
  • When you see a Lipschitz function integrated against α−β → ​∫fd(α−β)​≤Lip(f)W1​(α,β).
  • On Rd, if weak convergence holds but Wp​ does not converge → look for mass escaping to infinity (check the moments).

On R, does αn​=(1−n1​)δ0​+n1​δn​​ converge to δ0​ weakly? In W1​? In W2​?

Answer

Weakly: yes (same argument as the escaping mass). W1​=n1​n​=n−1/2→0: yes, and indeed the first moment n1​n​→0. W2​=(n1​⋅n)1/2=1: no, and indeed the second moment n1​⋅n=1→0. The board’s proposition, applied with p=1 and p=2, predicts exactly this.

5. The strong topology: total variation notes p. 3–4#

Total variation measures how much mass differs, wherever it is: it is the transport cost for the “blind” distance that charges 1 for any move, so it ignores how far mass travels — Diracs never converge for it, while they do for Wp​.

Definition and first examples#

On the board notes p. 3

Def (strong topology on M1+​(X)): the total variation (TV) norm of M1+​(X) is defined as

∥α−β∥TV​=∥f∥∞​≤1sup​∫fd(α−β)} dual norm of the L∞ norm on C(X).

ex: if α−β=fdx then ∥α−β∥TV​=∥f∥L1​; if α−β=∑ai​δxi​​ then ∥α−β∥TV​=∑∣ai​∣.

α−β
A signed measure: positive where α has more mass than β, negative where it has less. Its total mass is α(X)−β(X)=0.
sup∥f∥∞​≤1​
Look for the test function bounded by 1 that best separates α from β. Ideally, f=+1 where α is larger and f=−1 where β is larger: it collects the total amount of mass by which they differ, ∣α−β∣(X). This ideal f usually jumps, so it is not continuous; but continuous functions bounded by 1 can approach it as closely as we want, so the supremum over C(X) has the same value (it is approached, not always attained).
∣α−β∣(X)
The total mass of the absolute value of the signed measure α−β: add the excess of α over β (where α−β>0) and the excess of β over α (where α−β<0). For densities ∫∣ρα​−ρβ​∣, for histograms ∑i​∣ai​−bi​∣.
“dual norm”
The TV norm is to measures what the sup norm is to functions: it is the size of α−β seen as a linear form f↦∫fd(α−β) on (C(X),∥⋅∥∞​).
the two examples
In the first one, f is the density of the signed measure α−β, not a test function (the board uses the letter f for both); call it ρ=ρα​−ρβ​. The ideal test function is the sign of ρ, and ∥α−β∥TV​=∫∣ρ∣=∫∣ρα​−ρβ​∣. In the second, ai​ is the weight of α−β at xi​, and ∥α−β∥TV​=∑i​∣ai​∣.

For probability measures, 0≤∥α−β∥TV​≤2, and the value 2 is reached exactly when α and β live on disjoint sets (no overlap at all).

Worked example

On three points, a=(0.5,0.3,0.2) and b=(0.2,0.3,0.5). Then ∥a−b∥TV​=0.3+0+0.3=0.6. The best test function is f=(+1, anything, −1): ∑i​fi​(ai​−bi​)=0.3+0.3=0.6.

Total variation is a transport cost#

On the board notes p. 3

Prop: write d the 0/1 distance d(x,y)=1x=y​. Then  Wp​(α,β)p=21​∥α−β∥TV​.  ↪ proof as an exercise.

This is Exercise 1 of the sheet Wasserstein distances and duality:

Exercise sheet — Exercise 1 (total variation and 0/1 cost)

Let d(x,y)=1x=y​ be the discrete 0/1 distance. We wish to show that for any p≥1, and probability measures α and β, Wpp​(α,β)=21​∥α−β∥TV​. Start with two discrete probability measures α=∑i​ai​δxi​​ and β=∑i​bi​δxi​​ on the same finite set {xi​}i​, with weights a=(ai​) and b=(bi​) on the same support.

Intuition

With the 0/1 distance, moving a unit of mass costs 1, wherever it goes; leaving it in place costs 0. So the best plan leaves in place as much mass as possible and moves the rest anywhere it is needed. At the point xi​ at most min(ai​,bi​) can stay. The mass that must move is the excess of α over β, and ∥α−β∥TV​ counts each moved unit twice (once as an excess where it leaves, once as a deficit where it arrives): hence the 21​.

Full solution of Exercise 1
  1. dp=dfor every p≥1,soWpp​(α,β)=P∈U(a,b)min​i=j∑​Pij​=1−P∈U(a,b)max​i∑​Pii​.
    d only takes the values 0 and 1, and 0p=0, 1p=1. The cost of a plan is the mass it moves, i.e. 1 minus the mass ∑i​Pii​ it leaves in place. (This is why the answer does not depend on p.)
  2. For every plan, Pii​≤min(ai​,bi​), so ∑i​Pii​≤m:=∑i​min(ai​,bi​).Pii​ is one term of row i, which sums to ai​, and one term of column i, which sums to bi​ (all terms are ≥0).
  3. Let r=1−m. If r=0 then a=b and P=diag(a) keeps everything. Otherwise define
    P⋆=diag(min(a,b))+r(a−min(a,b))(b−min(a,b))⊤​.
    Keep the common part in place; send the excess of a to the deficit points of b, proportionally. (min(a,b) is taken entrywise.)
  4. P⋆ is a coupling: its entries are ≥0, and its row sums are
    ∑j​Pij⋆​​=min(ai​,bi​)+(ai​−min(ai​,bi​))r∑j​(bj​−min(aj​,bj​))​=min(ai​,bi​)+(ai​−min(ai​,bi​))r1−m​=ai​;​
    the column sums are bj​ in the same way.∑j​bj​=1 and ∑j​min(aj​,bj​)=m.
  5. P⋆ keeps exactly m in place: Pii⋆​=min(ai​,bi​).The second term of Pii⋆​ is (ai​−min(ai​,bi​))(bi​−min(ai​,bi​))/r=0: one of the two factors vanishes. So by step 2, P⋆ is optimal.
  6. Wpp​(α,β)=1−m​=i∑​2ai​+bi​​−i∑​min(ai​,bi​)=21​i∑​(ai​+bi​−2min(ai​,bi​))=21​i∑​∣ai​−bi​∣.​
    ∑i​ai​=∑i​bi​=1, and u+v−2min(u,v)=max(u,v)−min(u,v)=∣u−v∣.
  7. Wpp​(α,β)=21​∥α−β∥TV​.□
    The board’s second example of TV: for a discrete difference, ∥α−β∥TV​=∑i​∣ai​−bi​∣.

On the numbers of the worked example above: min(a,b)=(0.2,0.3,0.2), m=0.7, r=0.3; the excess (0.3,0,0) goes to the deficit (0,0,0.3), so P⋆=​0.200​00.30​0.300.2​​ and Wpp​=0.3=21​⋅0.6. (Checked against an exact LP solver, and on 500 random pairs of histograms.)

General measures. The same proof works with the common part α∧β in place of min(a,b): the largest measure that is below both α and β. For densities it has density min(ρα​,ρβ​); for histograms, weights min(ai​,bi​); in general one writes α and β with densities with respect to μ=α+β (they exist because α≤μ and β≤μ) and takes the minimum of the two densities. The diagonal of any coupling carries at most α∧β, and the plan “keep α∧β in place, move the rest by a product coupling” attains it.

Note on the sources: a factor 21​

Peyré–Cuturi, Computational Optimal Transport (Remark 2.26, p. 30) states that with the cost matrix 1n×n​−In​, LC​(a,b)=∥a−b∥1​. The correct value is 21​∥a−b∥1​, as on the board: for a=(1,0) and b=(0,1) the only coupling moves a mass 1 at cost 1, while ∥a−b∥1​=2. Watch out also for conventions: some books define the “total variation distance” as 21​∥α−β∥TV​ (values in [0,1]); this page always uses the board’s ∥α−β∥TV​=∣α−β∣(X) (values in [0,2]).

Diracs never converge for the strong topology#

On the board notes p. 3

Remark: ∥δxn​​−δx​∥TV​=2 (to check) if xn​=x, whereas Wp​(δxn​​,δx​)=d(xn​,x).

→ Dirac measures never converge for the strong topology.

Let us check the “2”. If xn​=x, the difference δxn​​−δx​ is a discrete signed measure with weight +1 at xn​ and −1 at x, so by the board’s formula ∥δxn​​−δx​∥TV​=∣+1∣+∣−1∣=2. With test functions: a continuous f with ∥f∥∞​≤1, f(xn​)=1 and f(x)=−1 exists (two small bumps of opposite signs), and gives ∫fd(δxn​​−δx​)=2, the largest possible value. With the proposition: for the 0/1 distance, Wpp​(δxn​​,δx​)=1, so 21​∥⋅∥TV​=1. Three ways, same answer. ✓

So however close xn​ is to x, the total variation stays at its maximum 2; it drops to 0 only if xn​=x exactly. Total variation only asks whether mass moved, never how far: it is the transport cost for a ground distance in which all distinct points are at distance 1. Wp​ uses the real distance d, and sees that δxn​​ is close to δx​.

Riemann sums: discrete measures converging to a density#

On the board notes p. 3, bottom, and p. 4, top

example. f continuous [0,1]→[a,b]:

n1​k=1∑n​f(nk​)⟶∫01​f(t)dt⟹n1​k=1∑n​δk/n​n→+∞​U[0,1]​,⟨f,n1​k=1∑n​δk/n​⟩→⟨f,U[0,1]​⟩.
Wp​(n1​k=1∑n​δk/n​, U[0,1]​)n→+∞​0.
⟨f,μ⟩
Duality bracket: ⟨f,μ⟩=∫fdμ. So ⟨f,n1​∑k​δk/n​⟩=n1​∑k​f(k/n), a Riemann sum, and ⟨f,U[0,1]​⟩=∫01​f.
U[0,1]​
The uniform law on [0,1] (density 1 on [0,1]).
the implication
Riemann sums of a continuous function converge to its integral: that is literally the statement that μn​=n1​∑k​δk/n​ converges weakly to U[0,1]​. Since [0,1] is compact, §4 then gives Wp​(μn​,U[0,1]​)→0.

We can do better than “→0”: we can compute the distance. On the line the optimal plan is monotone (refresher): the uniform mass on (nk−1​,nk​] goes to the atom nk​.

  1. Wpp​(μn​,U[0,1]​)=∫01​​Cμn​−1​(t)−t​pdt,Cμn​−1​(t)=nk​  for t∈(nk−1​,nk​].
    The quantile formula; the quantile function of U[0,1]​ is t↦t, that of μn​ is a staircase.
  2. =k=1∑n​∫(k−1)/nk/n​(nk​−t)pdt=n∫01/n​updu=n⋅p+1(1/n)p+1​=(p+1)np1​.
    Cut [0,1] into the n steps; on each, substitute u=nk​−t∈[0,n1​).
  3. Wp​(μn​,U[0,1]​)=n(p+1)−1/p​:W1​=2n1​,W2​=3​n1​.
    Take the p-th root. Both decay like 1/n.

And in total variation? μn​ lives on n points, a set of length zero, to which U[0,1]​ gives no mass. The two measures live on disjoint sets, so ​μn​−U[0,1]​​TV​=2 for every n. Discrete measures never converge in total variation to a measure with a density — which is the typical situation in machine learning, where data sets (finite samples) approximate continuous distributions. This is a strong argument for transport distances.

Strong versus weak: three sequences, four behaviours#

On a compact space, convergence in total variation implies convergence in Wp​: keeping the common part in place and moving the rest (at most 21​∥α−β∥TV​ of mass) over distances at most diam(X) gives Wpp​(α,β)≤diam(X)p⋅21​∥α−β∥TV​. The converse is false (Diracs, Riemann sums). On a non-compact space even the first implication fails (escaping mass).

sequence → limitweak∥αn​−α∥TV​W1​(αn​,α)W2​(αn​,α)
moving Dirac δ1/n​→δ0​yes21/n1/n
Riemann n1​∑k​δk/n​→U[0,1]​yes22n1​3​n1​
escaping (1−n1​)δ0​+n1​δn​→δ0​ (on R)yes2/n1n​

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: choose a sequence and move n. The top panel draws αn​ (orange-red) against its limit (blue); the bottom panel plots the three distances against n on log–log axes, where each power law is a straight line. For the escaping mass, the exponent slider moves the far atom to nγ: W1​=nγ−1 converges iff γ<1 and W2​=nγ−1/2 iff γ<21​, while the total variation 2/n does not care.

On a finite space the two topologies coincide (Exercise 2)#

Exercise sheet — Exercise 2 (equivalence of topologies on a finite discrete metric space)

Let (X,d) be a finite discrete metric space. Define dmin​:=minx=y​d(x,y) and dmax​:=maxx,y​d(x,y). Show that for all probability measures α,β on X,

2dmin​​∥α−β∥TV​ ≤ W1​(α,β) ≤ 2dmax​​∥α−β∥TV​.

Conclude that the W1​–topology and the total variation topology coincide on P(X).

Full solution of Exercise 2
  1. dmin​1x=y​ ≤ d(x,y) ≤ dmax​1x=y​for all x,y∈X.
    If x=y all three terms are 0. If x=y, d(x,y) lies between the smallest and the largest distance between distinct points. (Since X is finite with at least two points, 0<dmin​≤dmax​<∞.)
  2. For every coupling π:  dmin​∫1x=y​dπ≤∫ddπ≤dmax​∫1x=y​dπ.Integrate step 1 against π≥0.
  3. Lower bound. For every π, ∫ddπ≥dmin​∫1x=y​dπ≥dmin​⋅21​∥α−β∥TV​. Take the minimum over π: W1​(α,β)≥2dmin​​∥α−β∥TV​.∫1x=y​dπ is at least its minimum over couplings, which is 21​∥α−β∥TV​ by Exercise 1 with p=1.
  4. Upper bound. Let π⋆ be optimal for the 0/1 cost. Then W1​(α,β)≤∫ddπ⋆≤dmax​∫1x=y​dπ⋆=2dmax​​∥α−β∥TV​.π⋆ is admissible for W1​; step 2; Exercise 1.
  5. Conclusion. W1​ and ∥⋅∥TV​ are equivalent up to the constants 2dmin​​ and 2dmax​​: W1​(αn​,α)→0⟺∥αn​−α∥TV​→0. Same convergent sequences, same topology.Each one is bounded by a constant times the other.

Example. X={0,1,3}⊂R: dmin​=1, dmax​=3. For δ0​,δ1​: W1​=1=2dmin​​⋅2 (equality on the left). For δ0​,δ3​: W1​=3=2dmax​​⋅2 (equality on the right). For δ1​,δ3​: W1​=2, strictly in between.

Why this does not contradict the Diracs. On [0,1], distinct points can be arbitrarily close: “dmin​” would be 0 and the lower bound is empty. That is exactly the room in which δ1/n​→δ0​ in W1​ but not in TV. Finiteness of the space is what makes the two notions agree.

Reflexes
  • When you see ∥α−β∥TV​ → think “total mass that differs”; for mutually singular measures (e.g. discrete vs density) it is 2.
  • When the ground distance is 1x=y​ → transport = total variation: Wpp​=21​∥⋅∥TV​, keep the common part, move the rest.
  • To compare two transport costs with comparable ground costs c1​≤c2​ → integrate against a good coupling: Lc1​​≤Lc2​​.
Pitfall — “strong” is not “better”

Strong convergence (TV) is the more demanding notion, which makes it a worse notion for learning: an empirical distribution never gets close to a continuous one in TV. Weak convergence, measured by Wp​, is the one under which samples approximate their law.

Compute ​U[0,1]​−U[a,1+a]​​TV​ and W1​ between them, for 0<a<1.

Answer

The densities differ on [0,a) (only the first, value 1) and on (1,1+a] (only the second, value 1): ∥⋅∥TV​=∫∣ρ1​−ρ2​∣=a+a=2a. The monotone plan is the translation x↦x+a, so W1​=a. Here both go to 0 as a→0: shifting a density a little changes it a little in TV — unlike shifting a Dirac.

6. Displacement interpolation and geodesics notes p. 4#

To go from α to β, move every unit of mass along the straight segment from its starting point to its destination (given by an optimal plan) at constant speed: the distributions αt​ you see along the way form a shortest path for W2​.

The problem: how to go from one distribution to another?#

Between two points x and y of Rd the natural path is the segment (1−t)x+ty. Between two distributions there are two natural candidates, and they behave very differently.

Mixture (“vertical”)

mt​=(1−t)α+tβ. Nothing moves: the mass of α fades out where it is while the mass of β fades in where it is. For images: a cross-fade, with ghosting.

Displacement (“horizontal”)

Every unit of mass travels from its starting point x to its destination y, along the segment, at constant speed: at time t it is at (1−t)x+ty. For images: a morphing.

For the second one we need to know which x goes to which y: that is exactly what an optimal transport plan tells us.

Displacement interpolation#

On the board notes p. 4

Displacement interpolation. α,β∈M1+​(X),

Pt​(x,y)=(1−t)x+ty,P0​(x,y)=x,P1​(x,y)=y,
αt​:=Pt​#​π= distribution of (1−t)X+tY  where (X,Y)∼π.

[drawing: α0​=α, a set of concentric circles, deformed through αt​ into α1​=β, an irregular blob]

If π=(Id,T)#​α (Monge solution), then αt​ is the distribution of (1−t)X+tT(X) with X∼α.

αt​ = displacement interpolation, McCann.

π
An optimal plan between α and β for the quadratic cost ∥x−y∥2 (implicit on the board). It decides who goes where.
Pt​(x,y)
The point at fraction t of the way from x to y. At t=0 it is x, at t=1 it is y: P0​ and P1​ are the two projections of §1.
αt​=Pt​#​π
Take every pair (x,y) with its weight π, and put that weight at the intermediate point (1−t)x+ty. For a discrete plan, αt​=∑i,j​πij​δ(1−t)xi​+tyj​​.
endpoints
P0​(x,y)=x keeps the starting point and P1​(x,y)=y the arrival point, so α0​=α and α1​=β (the marginals of π). Beware a clash of names on the board: in §1, P1​ and P2​ were the first and second projections (the index was a coordinate); here the index of Pt​ is a time, so P0​ is the first projection and P1​ the second.
Monge case
If the optimal plan is a map, Y=T(X), then αt​=((1−t)Id+tT)#​α: every point x slides towards T(x). This is McCann’s interpolation (Lesson 1). By Brenier, this is the case when α has a density.
Worked examples
  • Two Diracs. α=δx​, β=δy​: the only plan is δ(x,y)​, so αt​=δ(1−t)x+ty​, a single atom sliding along the segment. The mixture instead is (1−t)δx​+tδy​: two atoms, fixed, changing weights.
  • A Dirac that splits. α=δ0​, β=21​δ−1​+21​δ1​ on R. The plan sends half of the mass to each side: αt​=21​δ−t​+21​δt​. Mass can split, because plans can.
  • Two Gaussians on the line. α=N(m0​,σ02​), β=N(m1​,σ12​). The optimal map is T(x)=m1​+σ0​σ1​​(x−m0​), so (1−t)X+tT(X) is again Gaussian with mean (1−t)m0​+tm1​ and standard deviation (1−t)σ0​+tσ1​:
    αt​=N((1−t)m0​+tm1​, ((1−t)σ0​+tσ1​)2).
    The standard deviations are interpolated linearly (not the variances). The mixture is a two-bump distribution as soon as the means are far apart.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: move t. The grey curve is the mixture mt​, the green one the displacement interpolation αt​ (computed by interpolating quantile functions, which on the line is exactly Pt​#​π for the monotone plan). The readout compares W2​(α,⋅) with tW2​(α,β): for αt​ the ratio is exactly 1 at every t (constant speed); for the mixture it is not. Try the pair with two bumps: αt​ moves the mass of one bump into both bumps of β.

Constant speed: W2​(αs​,αt​)=∣t−s∣W2​(α,β)#

This is the property that makes αt​ a “straight line” in the Wasserstein space: it travels at constant speed, and the distance covered between times s and t is proportional to t−s.

Proposition (constant speed) — on Rd with c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2

If π is optimal between α and β and αt​=Pt​#​π, then W2​(αs​,αt​)=∣t−s∣W2​(α,β) for all s,t∈[0,1].

Idea of the proof

Upper bound: follow the mass itself from time s to time t; it moves by (t−s) times its total displacement. Lower bound: if some piece of the path were a shortcut, the triangle inequality would make the whole trip shorter than W2​(α,β), which is impossible.

Full proof
  1. Let s≤t. The plan (Ps​,Pt​)#​π couples αs​ and αt​: under it, the mass that went x→y is matched from (1−s)x+sy to (1−t)x+ty.Its marginals are Ps​#​π=αs​ and Pt​#​π=αt​.
  2. W22​(αs​,αt​)≤∫∥Pt​(x,y)−Ps​(x,y)∥2dπ=∫∥(t−s)(y−x)∥2dπ=(t−s)2W22​(α,β).
    Any coupling gives an upper bound; Pt​−Ps​=(t−s)(y−x); π is optimal for α,β.
  3. So W2​(αs​,αt​)≤(t−s)W2​(α,β) for all s≤t. Apply it to the three pieces [0,s], [s,t], [t,1] and use the triangle inequality (§2):
    W2​(α,β)​≤W2​(α0​,αs​)+W2​(αs​,αt​)+W2​(αt​,α1​)≤(s+(t−s)+(1−t))W2​(α,β)=W2​(α,β).​
    The two ends of the chain are equal, so every inequality in between is an equality.
  4. In particular W2​(αs​,αt​)=(t−s)W2​(α,β).If it were strictly smaller, the middle sum would be strictly smaller than W2​(α,β).

A geodesic space#

On the board notes p. 4

Prop: (P2​(Rd),W2​) is a geodesic space.

Reminder: (X,d) is a geodesic space if for any (x,y)∈X2 there exists a shortest path (= geodesic) joining x and y: γ:[0,1]→X s.t. γ(0)=x, γ(1)=y and d(γ(s),γ(t))=∣s−t∣d(x,y).

γ:[0,1]→X
A path (a curve) in the space, parametrised by time. (On the board the letter γ is a path here, not the third measure of §2.)
d(γ(s),γ(t))=∣s−t∣d(x,y)
The path is a constant-speed shortest path: the distance covered between two times is proportional to the elapsed time, and the total length is exactly d(x,y). In Rd: the segment. On a sphere: an arc of great circle.
geodesic space
Any two points can be joined by such a path. Counter-example: the plane with the origin removed, R2∖{0}, between x and −x — the only candidate (the segment) goes through the missing point.
P2​(Rd)
Probability measures with a finite second moment, the natural home of W2​ on Rd (§2).

Proof of the proposition. Given α,β∈P2​(Rd), take an optimal plan π (it exists) and γ(t)=αt​. Then γ(0)=α, γ(1)=β, and the constant-speed proposition is exactly the condition W2​(αs​,αt​)=∣s−t∣W2​(α,β). □

Pitfall — the mixture is not a geodesic (it is infinitely long!)

Take two Diracs at distance 1 and the mixture mt​=(1−t)δx​+tδy​. Between ms​ and mt​ (s<t), the common part stays and an extra mass t−s must travel a distance 1: W2​(ms​,mt​)=t−s​, not t−s. Cut [0,1] into N equal pieces and add up the distances: N⋅1/N​=N​→∞. The mixture path has infinite length for W2​ (for N=4,16,64: lengths 2,4,8, while W2​(δx​,δy​)=1).

(For W1​ the mixture is a geodesic: W1​(ms​,mt​)=(t−s)W1​(α,β). Geodesics of W1​ are not unique. This is one reason why W2​ is the distance of choice for interpolation.)

αt​ is the weighted average of α and β#

On the board notes p. 4

We also have:  αt​∈ρargmin​ (1−t)W22​(α,ρ)+tW22​(β,ρ).

Why this matters. In Rd the point (1−t)x+ty is the minimiser of z↦(1−t)∥z−x∥2+t∥z−y∥2 (set the gradient 2(1−t)(z−x)+2t(z−y) to zero). The board says that the same characterisation holds in the Wasserstein space: αt​ is the weighted average of α and β, with weights (1−t,t), defined variationally. This is the bridge to the next section: averaging more than two distributions.

Proof (an algebraic identity and the triangle inequality)

Fix ρ and write A=W2​(α,ρ), B=W2​(ρ,β), D=W2​(α,β).

  1. (1−t)A2+tB2=t(1−t)(A+B)2+((1−t)A−tB)2.
    Expand the right side: t(1−t)(A2+2AB+B2)+(1−t)2A2−2t(1−t)AB+t2B2=(1−t)A2+tB2.
  2. (1−t)A2+tB2 ≥ t(1−t)(A+B)2 ≥ t(1−t)D2.
    Drop the square ≥0; then the triangle inequality A+B≥D (§2).
  3. For ρ=αt​: A=tD and B=(1−t)D (constant speed), so (1−t)A2+tB2=(1−t)t2D2+t(1−t)2D2=t(1−t)D2.The lower bound of step 2 is attained.
  4. Hence αt​ minimises ρ↦(1−t)W22​(α,ρ)+tW22​(β,ρ), with minimal value t(1−t)W22​(α,β).Step 2 holds for every ρ.

(Conversely, any minimiser must turn both inequalities into equalities, so it sits on some geodesic at the right fraction t: when α has a density, the minimiser is unique and it is αt​.)

Reflexes
  • To interpolate between two distributions → interpolate positions along an optimal plan, not weights.
  • To compute αt​ on the line → average quantile functions: Cαt​−1​=(1−t)Cα−1​+tCβ−1​.
  • To prove that something is a geodesic → upper bound by a coupling, then the triangle inequality forces equality.

Compute the displacement interpolation between U[0,1]​ and U[2,4]​.

Answer

The monotone map is T(x)=2+2x. With X∼U[0,1]​: (1−t)X+t(2+2X)=2t+(1+t)X, uniform on [2t, 2t+1+t]=[2t, 1+3t]. At t=0: [0,1]; at t=1: [2,4]; the length grows linearly from 1 to 2.

7. Wasserstein barycenters notes p. 4–5#

The average of points is the point that minimises the weighted sum of squared distances to them; replacing points by distributions and the distance by a transport cost defines the average of distributions — the Wasserstein barycenter.

Barycenters of points, and the Fréchet mean#

On the board notes p. 4

Wasserstein barycenters. x1​,…,xP​ points in Rd,  λ1​,…,λP​≥0,  ∑λk​=1,  x⋆=∑λk​xk​:

B(x1​,…,xP​)=xargmin​ k=1∑P​λk​c(x,xk​)∥x−xk​∥2​​

c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2 → weighted mean; c(x,y)=∥x−y∥ → weighted median.

[drawing: points on a curved surface] → “Fréchet mean”.  → Generalization to proba measures?

Why the mean minimises squared distances. F(x)=∑k​λk​∥x−xk​∥2 is a strictly convex quadratic; its gradient ∇F(x)=2∑k​λk​(x−xk​)=2(x−∑k​λk​xk​) vanishes only at x⋆=∑k​λk​xk​ (we used ∑k​λk​=1). So the barycenter is the weighted mean.

Changing the cost changes the average. With c(x,y)=∥x−y∥ (not squared), the minimiser is the (weighted, geometric) median. On R with points 0,1,10 and equal weights: the mean is 11/3≈3.67, pulled by the outlier 10; the median is 1. Squaring the distance punishes large distances, so the mean compromises with the outlier; the median does not.

The Fréchet mean. The variational definition has a big advantage: it needs no addition. On a curved space — a circle, a sphere, a surface — you cannot form ∑k​λk​xk​ (it leaves the space), but you can still minimise ∑k​λk​d(x,xk​)2 with the distance d of the space. That minimiser is the Fréchet mean. The board’s drawing shows points on a curved surface: their Euclidean average falls outside it; the Fréchet mean stays on it.

The idea of the lecture: the space of probability measures with W2​ is such a “curved” space. Distributions can be added (the mixture ∑k​λk​βk​ is a distribution), but this linear average is the average for a different geometry: it minimises ∑k​λk​∥ρ−ρk​∥L22​ over densities, a geometry that does not move mass. To average shapes and positions, use the Fréchet mean for W2​.

Definition#

On the board notes p. 4

β1​,…,βP​ proba measures,  λ1​,…,λP​≥0,  ∑λk​=1:

B(β1​,…,βP​)∈α∈M1+​argmin​ k=1∑P​λk​Lc​(α,βk​)(ex: Lc​=Wpp​).

ex: βk​=δxk​​ ⇒  solution δB(x1​,…,xP​)​.

β1​,…,βP​
The input distributions (for instance P images, P data sets, P shapes).
λk​
How much each input counts. λ=(1−t,t) with P=2 gives the geodesic of §6. An input with λk​=0 does not count at all and can be dropped.
Lc​(α,βk​)
The transport cost from the candidate average α to the k-th input. The standard choice is W22​ on Rd.
“∈argmin”
The minimiser need not be unique (see below), hence “∈”.
Worked example — the barycenter of Diracs is the Dirac at the barycenter
  1. Lc​(α,δxk​​)=∫c(x,xk​)dα(x).
    The only coupling of α and δxk​​ sends all the mass to xk​ (§1, quick check).
  2. k∑​λk​Lc​(α,δxk​​)=∫F(x)dα(x),F(x)=k∑​λk​c(x,xk​).
    Linearity of the integral.
  3. ∫Fdα ≥ minF,
    with equality if and only if α puts all its mass on the minimisers of F.An average of a function is at least its minimum.
  4. So the barycenter is δx⋆​ with x⋆=argminF=B(x1​,…,xP​) — the weighted mean for c=∥⋅∥2.When F has a unique minimiser, δx⋆​ is the only distribution concentrated on it.

Compare with the mixture ∑k​λk​δxk​​: it keeps P separate atoms. The Wasserstein barycenter merges them into one atom at the average position. This is what “averaging positions instead of weights” means.

Histograms on a common grid: a linear program#

On the board notes p. 5, top

ex: βk​ discrete histograms on the same grid,

α discreteon the same grid​min​ k=1∑P​λk​Wpp​(α,βk​) ⟶ LP
α,P1​,…,PP​min​{k∑​λk​⟨Pk​,Dp⟩ : ∀k, Pk​1grid​=α,  Pk⊤​1grid​=βk​}

[drawing: a small grid of points, two of them marked by crosses]

the grid
Fixed points g1​,…,gn​ (pixels of an image, bins of a histogram). All inputs and the unknown barycenter are weight vectors on these points: α,βk​∈R+n​, summing to 1.
Dp
The matrix of the p-th powers of the distances between grid points, (Dp)ij​=d(gi​,gj​)p.
Pk​
A transport plan from the barycenter α to the input βk​ (n×n matrix). Pk​1=α: its row sums are α; Pk⊤​1=βk​: its column sums are βk​. (Careful: on the board the letter P is also the number of inputs; P1​,…,PP​ are the P plans.)
⟨Pk​,Dp⟩
∑ij​(Pk​)ij​d(gi​,gj​)p, the cost of the plan Pk​.
“→ LP”
Minimising over α of a sum of minima over plans is the same as minimising jointly over (α,P1​,…,PP​). The objective is linear in these unknowns, the constraints are linear equalities plus Pk​≥0: a linear program.

Size. The unknowns are n+Pn2 numbers. For P=3 images of 100×100 pixels, n=104 and Pn2=3×108: far too large for a generic LP solver. In practice one adds an entropic regularization and uses Sinkhorn-type iterations (Lesson 7).

Worked example — what a fixed grid does to the barycenter

Grid {0,1,2,3,4}⊂R, inputs β1​=δ0​, β2​=δ3​, weights 21​,21​, p=2. By the Dirac computation above, a candidate α pays ∫Fdα with F(x)=21​x2+21​(x−3)2. On the grid, F=(4.5, 2.5, 2.5, 4.5, 8.5).

  • The true barycenter δ1.5​ (value F(1.5)=2.25) is not on the grid.
  • The grid barycenters are all the α carried by {1,2} (value 2.5): δ1​, δ2​, 21​δ1​+21​δ2​, … — infinitely many. An LP solver returns one of them (δ1​ in our test).

A fixed grid approximates the barycenter only up to the grid resolution, and can create artificial non-uniqueness and blur.

Existence and uniqueness (Agueh–Carlier)#

On the board notes p. 5

[Agueh, Carlier 2010]  X=Rd, W2​:

  • → existence of solution;
  • → uniqueness if one βk​ is A.C.
Agueh–Carlier
M. Agueh and G. Carlier, Barycenters in the Wasserstein space, SIAM J. Math. Anal. 43(2), 2011 (preprint 2010). The paper that introduced Wasserstein barycenters for W2​ on Rd (inputs in P2​(Rd)).
A.C.
Absolutely continuous (with respect to Lebesgue measure): has a density. One input with a density and a positive weight λk​>0 is enough for uniqueness. (An input with weight 0 plays no role: adding a Gaussian with weight 0 to the non-uniqueness example below leaves it non-unique.)
Worked example — without densities, uniqueness can fail

In R2, β1​=21​(δ(−1,0)​+δ(1,0)​) and β2​=21​(δ(0,−1)​+δ(0,1)​), weights 21​,21​. Every point of β1​ is at squared distance 2 from every point of β2​, so every coupling is optimal and W22​(β1​,β2​)=2. By §6 the barycenter value is at least 21​⋅21​⋅2=21​.

  • Pair (−1,0) with (0,−1) and (1,0) with (0,1), and take midpoints: αA​=21​(δ(−21​,−21​)​+δ(21​,21​)​). Each atom is at squared distance 21​ from its two partners: value 21​. Optimal.
  • The other pairing gives αB​=21​(δ(−21​,21​)​+δ(21​,−21​)​), also of value 21​. Optimal too.
  • Their mixture (uniform on the four points (±21​,±21​)) also has value 21​: infinitely many barycenters.

The non-uniqueness comes from the non-uniqueness of the optimal plan between the inputs. A density on one input forces optimal plans to be maps (Brenier) and removes this freedom.

A useful fact: the mean of the barycenter is the barycenter of the means

For W22​ on Rd, any barycenter α⋆ has mean ∫xdα⋆=∑k​λk​∫xdβk​.

Why (the mean–shape decomposition of W2​)

For any coupling, write x=mα​+u and y=mβ​+v with u,v centred. Then ∥x−y∥2=∥mα​−mβ​∥2+2⟨mα​−mβ​,u−v⟩+∥u−v∥2, and the middle term integrates to 0. Translations do not change the set of couplings of the centred measures, so

W22​(α,β)=∥mα​−mβ​∥2+W22​(α~,β~​),

where α~,β~​ are the centred versions. In the barycenter objective, the mean mα​ only appears in ∑k​λk​∥mα​−mβk​​∥2, minimised by the mean of the means (barycenter of points!), while the shape part does not depend on mα​. This is also why, for Gaussians (§8), means and covariances separate.

Pitfall — barycenter ≠ mixture

The mixture ∑k​λk​βk​ is a distribution, it is “an average”, and it is easy to compute — but it is not the Wasserstein barycenter. Two Diracs: mixture = two atoms; barycenter = one atom in the middle. Two Gaussians: mixture = two bumps; barycenter = one Gaussian.

On R, what is the barycenter of δ0​,δ1​,δ10​ with weights (0.2,0.2,0.6), for c=∣x−y∣2? For c=∣x−y∣?

Answer

Quadratic cost: δx⋆​ with x⋆=0.2⋅0+0.2⋅1+0.6⋅10=6.2. Absolute cost: the weighted median; more than half of the weight sits at 10, so the minimiser of 0.2∣x∣+0.2∣x−1∣+0.6∣x−10∣ is x=10: the barycenter is δ10​.

8. Two cases with closed forms: Gaussians and the line notes p. 5#

The barycenter of Gaussians is the Gaussian whose mean is the average of the means and whose covariance solves a matrix fixed-point equation; on the line, the barycenter is obtained by averaging quantile functions.

Gaussian inputs#

On the board notes p. 5

Gaussians: βk​=N(mk​,Σk​) and c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2.

Prop: the barycenter is a Gaussian N(m⋆,Σ⋆) with

m⋆=k=1∑P​λk​mk​andΣ⋆∈Σargmin​ k=1∑P​λk​B(Σ,Σk​)2,
B(Σ,Λ)2=tr(Σ+Λ−2(Λ1/2ΣΛ1/2)1/2).

→Σ⋆ is also the unique solution of the fixed point problem:

Σ⋆=Ψ(Σ⋆)whereΨ(Σ)=k=1∑P​λk​(Σ1/2Σk​Σ1/2)1/2.

→ Fixed-point algo:  Σ(ℓ+1)=Ψ(Σ(ℓ)). [drawing: ellipses]

N(m,Σ)
Gaussian with mean m and covariance Σ (symmetric positive matrix). Picture: an ellipse centred at m, axes along the eigenvectors of Σ, half-lengths ∝ square roots of the eigenvalues — the ellipses of the board’s drawing.
B(Σ,Λ)
The Bures distance between covariance matrices (Lesson 1): W22​(N(m,Σ),N(m′,Λ))=∥m−m′∥2+B(Σ,Λ)2.
M1/2
Matrix square root (diagonalise, take the square roots of the eigenvalues). See the refresher.
Ψ
A map from covariance matrices to covariance matrices; the barycenter covariance is a fixed point of it.
“the unique solution”
Unique among positive definite matrices, as soon as one input with λk​>0 has a positive definite Σk​. The zero matrix is always a (useless) fixed point, since Ψ(0)=0; this is why the algorithm starts from a positive definite Σ(0).
Σ(ℓ)
The ℓ-th iterate of the algorithm, starting from any positive definite Σ(0).

Why the means and covariances separate

Try a Gaussian candidate α=N(m,Σ) in the barycenter objective, using the Gaussian formula for each term:

k∑​λk​W22​(N(m,Σ),βk​)=only depends on mk∑​λk​∥m−mk​∥2​​+only depends on Σk∑​λk​B(Σ,Σk​)2​​.

Minimise each part separately: the first is the barycenter of the points mk​ (§7), so m⋆=∑k​λk​mk​; the second is the “Bures barycenter” problem of the board.

Why is the barycenter Gaussian at all (and not only the best Gaussian)?

The key fact is Gelbrich’s inequality: for any α,β with means mα​,mβ​ and covariances Σα​,Σβ​,

W22​(α,β) ≥ ∥mα​−mβ​∥2+B(Σα​,Σβ​)2,

with equality when both are Gaussian. So if you replace any candidate α by the Gaussian N(mα​,Σα​) with the same mean and covariance, each term W22​(α,βk​) (with βk​ Gaussian) can only decrease: Gaussian candidates are never worse. A barycenter exists (Agueh–Carlier), hence a Gaussian one exists; if one Σk​ with λk​>0 is positive definite, that βk​ has a density, the barycenter is unique, and therefore it is that Gaussian.

The one-dimensional case: average the standard deviations

In 1D, B(σ2,σk2​)2=σ2+σk2​−2σσk​=(σ−σk​)2. So the covariance problem is minσ​∑k​λk​(σ−σk​)2, whose solution is the mean of the standard deviations:

σ⋆=k∑​λk​σk​.
Worked example

β1​=N(0,1), β2​=N(4,9) (standard deviations 1 and 3), weights 21​,21​: the barycenter is N(2,22)=N(2,4).

  • Not the average of the variances (which would give variance 5).
  • Not the mixture 21​N(0,1)+21​N(4,9), which is not even Gaussian (its variance is 5+4=9: the average variance plus the spread of the means).

When all the Σk​ commute (for instance all diagonal), the same thing happens eigenvalue by eigenvalue: (Σ⋆)1/2=∑k​λk​Σk1/2​ — “average the square roots”. In general the matrices do not commute, and the fixed-point equation is the right generalisation.

Where the fixed-point equation comes from

Intuition — “the average of the transport maps is the identity”

From the barycenter α⋆=N(m⋆,Σ), the optimal map to βk​ is affine (Lesson 1): Tk​(x)=mk​+Ak​(x−m⋆) with Ak​=Σ−1/2(Σ1/2Σk​Σ1/2)1/2Σ−1/2. We will see in §9 that a barycenter is characterised by “on average, the points do not need to move”:

k∑​λk​Tk​(x)=xfor all x⟺k∑​λk​mk​=m⋆  and  k∑​λk​Ak​=I.

Multiply ∑k​λk​Ak​=I by Σ1/2 on both sides: ∑k​λk​(Σ1/2Σk​Σ1/2)1/2=Σ, i.e. Ψ(Σ)=Σ. The board’s fixed-point equation says exactly: the average of the optimal maps from the barycenter to the inputs is the identity.

The same equation by differentiation (first-order condition)

Write E(Σ)=∑k​λk​B(Σ,Σk​)2=trΣ+∑k​λk​trΣk​−2∑k​λk​tr(Σk1/2​ΣΣk1/2​)1/2. One can show that the derivative of Σ↦tr(Σk1/2​ΣΣk1/2​)1/2 in a symmetric direction Z is 21​tr(Ak​Z), with the matrix Ak​ above (compact notes, proof of Prop. 12.6). Hence

DE(Σ)[Z]=tr((I−∑k​λk​Ak​)Z),

which vanishes for all Z iff ∑k​λk​Ak​=I, i.e. Ψ(Σ)=Σ. E is convex, so this stationary point is the minimiser.

The fixed-point algorithm — and a faster cousin

The board’s algorithm iterates Σ(ℓ+1)=Ψ(Σ(ℓ)). Let us run it in 1D, where Ψ(v)=∑k​λk​vσk2​​=v​σˉ with σˉ=∑k​λk​σk​. On the worked example (σˉ=2), starting from the variance v(0)=1:

v(ℓ):1,  2,  2.83,  3.36,  3.67,  3.83,  3.91,  3.96, … ⟶ 4=(σ⋆)2.

It converges, but slowly: in terms of σ=v​, the update is σ←σσˉ​, so logσ moves halfway to logσˉ at each step — the error is only halved.

What is known about convergence

Peyré–Cuturi (Computational OT, Remark 9.5) note that Ψ is not a strict contraction, and that the iteration Σ←Ψ(Σ) “converges in practice” (we observed convergence on 800 random instances in dimensions 2 to 10, sometimes after more than 200 iterations). Álvarez-Esteban, del Barrio, Cuesta-Albertos and Matrán (2016) proposed the variant

Σ(ℓ+1)=(Σ(ℓ))−1/2Ψ(Σ(ℓ))2(Σ(ℓ))−1/2,

for which convergence is proved, and which is much faster: in 1D it gives v←(v​σˉ)2/v=σˉ2, the exact answer in one step. This variant is not a trick: it is exactly the general algorithm of the board’s last paragraph (§9), run on Gaussians.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: three Gaussians in the plane (blue ellipses: one standard deviation). Drag the green dot inside the triangle to choose the weights λ (the closer to a corner, the more that input counts); the green ellipse is the barycenter N(m⋆,Σ⋆). Near a corner it becomes that input; in the middle, a compromise of shapes (orientations and elongations), not a superposition. The small plot on the right runs both iterations from Σ(0)=I and shows the Bures distance to Σ⋆ (log scale): the board’s Ψ iteration (grey, dashed) and the Álvarez-Esteban update (green, solid). The menu draws the first iterates Σ(0),…,Σ(5) as ellipses.

Measures on the line: average the quantiles#

On the board notes p. 5

1D case:

k∑​λk​W22​(α,βk​)=k∑​λk​∫01​​Cα−1​(t)−Cβk​−1​(t)​2dt
⇒ ∀t,Cα−1​(t)=k=1∑P​λk​Cβk​−1​(t).

[drawing: two CDFs Cβ1​​, Cβ2​​ on [0,1]]

Cα​, Cα−1​
CDF and quantile function of α (refresher). Cα−1​(t) = the position of the t-th quantile.
first line
The 1D formula W22​(α,β)=∫01​​Cα−1​−Cβ−1​​2, used for each input.
“⇒”
The unknown α only enters through its quantile function q=Cα−1​, and the objective is ∫01​(∑k​λk​∣q(t)−qk​(t)∣2)dt. Minimise separately for each t: for fixed t this is the barycenter of the points q1​(t),…,qP​(t) with weights λ, i.e. their weighted mean.
Detail: the average of quantile functions is a quantile function

Pointwise minimisation is legitimate only if the result q=∑k​λk​qk​ is itself the quantile function of a probability measure. It is: quantile functions are exactly the non-decreasing, left-continuous functions on (0,1), and a positive combination of such functions is again one. (Its square-integrability follows from that of each qk​.) So q is admissible, and it minimises the integrand at every t, hence the integral.
