Intuition — average horizontally, not vertically

On a graph of CDFs (like the board’s drawing), the barycenter is obtained by averaging horizontally: at each height t, put the new curve at the average of the abscissas where the input CDFs reach t. Averaging vertically (averaging the values Cβk​​(x) at each x) gives the CDF of the mixture. Horizontal = move mass; vertical = mix mass.

Worked examples
  • Two uniforms. β1​=U[0,1]​, β2​=U[2,4]​, weights 21​,21​. Quantiles: q1​(t)=t, q2​(t)=2+2t. Average: 1+23​t, the quantile function of U[1,2.5]​. (The mixture would be two separate blocks.)
  • Gaussians. With Φ the CDF of N(0,1), qk​(t)=mk​+σk​Φ−1(t), so ∑k​λk​qk​=mˉ+σˉΦ−1: the Gaussian N(mˉ,σˉ2) with σˉ=∑k​λk​σk​ — the same answer as the Gaussian proposition, as it should.
  • Diracs. qk​≡xk​, so the average is the constant ∑k​λk​xk​: the Dirac at the mean (§7).
  • A uniform and a Dirac. β1​=U[0,1]​, β2​=δ3​, weights 21​,21​: 21​t+23​, the quantile function of U[1.5,2]​ — the uniform is moved halfway and shrunk by half.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: choose a pair of inputs and move the weight λ (the barycenter is λ-close to β2​). Top: densities — the green barycenter is always a single “shape” that travels and morphs between the inputs, while the grey dashed mixture is a superposition. Bottom: the CDFs, with the horizontal averaging at a few levels. Two bumps against one bump: the barycenter keeps two bumps whose positions and widths interpolate.

Reflexes
  • Gaussian inputs, quadratic cost → barycenter is Gaussian; mean = average of means; covariance = fixed point of Ψ (in 1D: average of standard deviations).
  • Inputs on the line → average the quantile functions.
  • To check a barycenter formula → test it on Diracs (it must give the Dirac at the mean) and on Gaussians.
Pitfall — averaging the wrong thing

Averaging densities or CDFs gives the mixture. Averaging variances gives the wrong width. For W2​ barycenters, average positions: quantiles in 1D, standard deviations for 1D Gaussians, square roots of commuting covariances.

Barycenter of N(0,1) and N(4,9) with weights λ=(41​,43​), and its objective value?

Answer

m⋆=41​⋅0+43​⋅4=3, σ⋆=41​⋅1+43​⋅3=2.5: the barycenter is N(3,6.25). Value: ∑k​λk​[(m⋆−mk​)2+(σ⋆−σk​)2]=41​(9+2.25)+43​(1+0.25)=2.8125+0.9375=3.75.

9. How to compute barycenters: the fixed-point algorithm notes p. 5#

From the current guess α, compute the optimal maps Tk​ to each input, average them into T=∑k​λk​Tk​, and move α by T; each step decreases the barycenter cost, and a barycenter is a point where the averaged map is the identity.

On the board notes p. 5, bottom

How to compute them?

[drawing: a measure α in the middle, arrows T1​,T2​,T3​ to β1​,β2​,β3​, and the measure T(α)#​α]

Tk​#​α(ℓ)=βk​,T(α)=k=1∑P​λk​Tk​with Tk​=OT(α,βk​).

T(α) is itself an optimal map between α and T(α)#​α.

α(ℓ+1):=T(α(ℓ))#​α(ℓ).
setting
Rd, quadratic cost ∥x−y∥2, and a current guess α(ℓ) with a density, so that optimal maps exist (Brenier). When the inputs βk​ have densities, every step keeps a density (Álvarez-Esteban et al., 2016), so the maps exist at every iteration. This can fail otherwise: if all inputs are Diracs, T is constant and α(1) is a Dirac — the right answer here, but maps from a Dirac no longer make sense. For point clouds, assignments replace maps (end of this section).
Tk​=OT(α,βk​)
The optimal transport map from the current α to the k-th input: Tk​#​α=βk​.
T(α)=∑k​λk​Tk​
The averaged map: the point x is sent to the weighted average of its P destinations T1​(x),…,TP​(x). The superscript (α) recalls that the maps depend on the current α.
α(ℓ+1)
The new guess: move the mass of α(ℓ) with the averaged map.

The idea, with points#

For points, the barycenter is found in one step: wherever you start, move to ∑k​λk​xk​. Here “where does x go in each input” is the information carried by the maps Tk​(x), and moving to ∑k​λk​Tk​(x) is the same move. The difference with points: once α has moved, the optimal maps from the new α are different, so we iterate. The algorithm stops moving when the averaged map is the identity: on average, every point is already where its destinations want it to be. That is the “no net displacement” condition we used for Gaussians in §8.

Why T(α) is an optimal map#

  1. By Brenier, Tk​=∇φk​ with φk​ convex.Tk​ is the optimal map for the quadratic cost from a measure with a density.
  2. T(α)=k∑​λk​∇φk​=∇(k∑​λk​φk​).
    The gradient is linear.
  3. ∑k​λk​φk​ is convex, so T(α) is the gradient of a convex function, hence the optimal map between α and T(α)#​α.A positive combination of convex functions is convex; and the converse part of Brenier: the gradient of any convex function is optimal between a measure and its push-forward.

So the board’s remark says: the step from α(ℓ) to α(ℓ+1) is itself an optimal transport, and its cost is W22​(α(ℓ),α(ℓ+1))=∫​x−T(α)(x)​2dα(ℓ)(x).

Why the algorithm works: each step decreases the cost#

Proposition (descent) — Álvarez-Esteban et al. 2016; Zemel–Panaretos 2019

Let F(α)=∑k​λk​W22​(α,βk​) be the barycenter cost, T=T(α) the averaged map. Then

F(T#​α) ≤ F(α)−∫∥x−T(x)∥2dα(x) = F(α)−W22​(α,T#​α).
Idea of the proof

A Pythagoras-type identity for points (“the mean is the closest point on average”), applied at every x to the P destinations Tk​(x), then integrated; the new measure is coupled to each input through the old one.

Full proof
  1. For points y1​,…,yP​ with mean yˉ​=∑k​λk​yk​ and any z:
    k∑​λk​∥z−yk​∥2=∥z−yˉ​∥2+k∑​λk​∥yˉ​−yk​∥2.
    Write z−yk​=(z−yˉ​)+(yˉ​−yk​) and expand: the cross term 2⟨z−yˉ​,∑k​λk​(yˉ​−yk​)⟩ vanishes because ∑k​λk​(yˉ​−yk​)=0. (The variance decomposition.)
  2. Apply it at each x with z=x, yk​=Tk​(x), yˉ​=T(x), and integrate against α:
    k∑​λk​∫∥x−Tk​(x)∥2dα=∫∥x−T(x)∥2dα+k∑​λk​∫∥T(x)−Tk​(x)∥2dα.
    Integration of an identity valid at every point.
  3. The left side is F(α).Tk​ is optimal from α to βk​, so ∫∥x−Tk​(x)∥2dα=W22​(α,βk​).
  4. For each k, ∫∥T(x)−Tk​(x)∥2dα ≥ W22​(T#​α,βk​); so the last sum is ≥F(T#​α).With X∼α, the pair (T(X),Tk​(X)) is a coupling of T#​α and Tk​#​α=βk​ — a gluing through the old measure. Any coupling gives an upper bound on W22​.
  5. F(α) ≥ ∫∥x−T(x)∥2dα+F(T#​α),
    and ∫∥x−T(x)∥2dα=W22​(α,T#​α).Steps 2–4; the last equality because T is optimal (previous subsection).

Three consequences.

  • Descent. Each step decreases the cost by at least the squared length of the step: the algorithm never goes uphill. (It is in fact a gradient descent with step 1 in the Wasserstein space; Zemel–Panaretos, 2019.)
  • Barycenters are fixed points. If α is a barycenter, F(T#​α)≥F(α), so ∫∥x−T(x)∥2dα=0:  ∑k​λk​Tk​=Id (α-almost everywhere). This is the first-order optimality condition of Agueh and Carlier, and the condition used for Gaussians in §8.
  • Convergence of the iterates to the barycenter holds under regularity assumptions (Álvarez-Esteban et al., 2016; Zemel–Panaretos, 2019) — a harder theorem, not proved here.

Three special cases#

On the line: exact in one step

From α (with a continuous CDF), the optimal maps are Tk​=Cβk​−1​∘Cα​. The quantile function of T#​α is T∘Cα−1​=∑k​λk​Cβk​−1​∘Cα​∘Cα−1​=∑k​λk​Cβk​−1​ — the barycenter of §8, whatever the starting point. One step, as for points.

Gaussians: the Álvarez-Esteban update

Start from α=N(m,Σ). The optimal maps are Tk​(x)=mk​+Ak​(x−m) with Ak​=Σ−1/2(Σ1/2Σk​Σ1/2)1/2Σ−1/2. Average them:

T(x)=m⋆+A(x−m),A=k∑​λk​Ak​=Σ−1/2Ψ(Σ)Σ−1/2,

with m⋆=∑k​λk​mk​. An affine image of a Gaussian is Gaussian: T#​α=N(m⋆,AΣA), and

AΣA=Σ−1/2Ψ(Σ)Σ−1/2ΣΣ−1/2Ψ(Σ)Σ−1/2=Σ−1/2Ψ(Σ)2Σ−1/2.

So the general algorithm, run on Gaussians, is exactly the provably convergent update of §8. The mean is right after one step; the covariance converges fast (in the widget of §8, about 5× closer at each step on the default example, against 2× for the board’s Ψ iteration).

Point clouds: average the matched partners

If the current guess and every input are clouds of n points with equal weights n1​, optimal plans can be taken to be permutations (Lesson 2, Birkhoff–von Neumann): the optimal “map” Tk​ sends the point xi​ to its partner yσk​(i)k​ in the optimal assignment. The step is then

xi​ ← k∑​λk​yσk​(i)k​(each point moves to the average of its partners).

The descent proof applies verbatim (step 4 only needs couplings). Since there are finitely many assignments and the cost strictly decreases while points move, the iteration stops after finitely many steps, at a fixed point. Caveat: for point clouds the problem is not convex in the positions, so different starting clouds can stop at slightly different fixed points. In the widget below, starting from the ring gives a fixed point of cost 9.4819 after two steps, and starting from the first random cloud gives 9.4834 after four.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: three input clouds (blue) and the current guess α(ℓ) (green). Press Step: each green point is matched to one point of each input (optimal assignment), the thin lines show where its partners are, and it moves to their weighted average. The readout prints the cost F before and after, and the squared step length: you can check the descent inequality at every step. Typically the cloud settles after 2 to 5 steps. Move the weights to get other barycenters; restart from a random cloud to see the fixed point (and its cost) change slightly.

Other ways to compute barycenters (beyond this lecture)
  • Fixed grid: the linear program of §7, or, much faster, its entropic regularisation solved by Sinkhorn-like iterations (Lesson 7).
  • Free support: the fixed-point algorithm above, with barycentric projections when the clouds have different sizes (Cuturi–Doucet, 2014).
  • Multi-marginal formulation: for the quadratic cost, the barycenter is the push-forward of an optimal multi-marginal plan by (x1​,…,xP​)↦∑k​λk​xk​ (compact notes, Prop. 12.16).
Reflexes
  • Barycenter condition → “the average of the optimal maps from the barycenter is the identity”.
  • Barycenter algorithm → average the maps, push the measure, repeat.
  • To show a step decreases a sum of squared distances → variance decomposition around the mean.

Why does the algorithm need the current guess α(ℓ) to have a density (or to be a cloud of n equal-weight points)?

Answer

To have optimal maps Tk​: averaging plans that split mass is not defined pointwise. With a density, Brenier gives maps; with equal-weight clouds of the same size, optimal permutations exist. (For general discrete measures one replaces Tk​(x) by the barycentric projection of the plan, the average of the destinations of x.)

10. Exercises#

The two exercises of the sheet that belong to this lecture (TV and 0/1 cost; finite spaces) are solved in full in §5: Exercise 1 and Exercise 2. (Exercise 3 of the sheet, on c-transforms, belongs to the next lecture.) Here are more, graded from ★ (direct application) to ★★★ (needs an idea). Try before opening the hint; open the hint before the solution.

Exercise 1 — Diracs and atoms ★

On R, compute (a) Wp​(δ0​,21​δ−1​+21​δ1​) for every p≥1; (b) W2​(21​δ0​+21​δ1​, 21​δ2​+21​δ3​).

Hint

(a) How many couplings are there with a Dirac? (b) On the line, the optimal plan is monotone.

Solution

(a) The only coupling sends half of the mass to −1 and half to 1, both at distance 1: Wpp​=21​⋅1+21​⋅1=1, so Wp​=1 for every p. (b) Monotone plan: 0→2, 1→3, each with mass 21​ and displacement 2: W22​=21​⋅4+21​⋅4=4, W2​=2. (The crossed plan 0→3, 1→2 would cost 21​(9+1)=5.)

Exercise 2 — Translations ★

Let α∈Pp​(Rd), v∈Rd and τv​(x)=x+v. Show that Wp​(α,τv​#​α)=∥v∥.

Hint

Upper bound: one coupling. Lower bound: Wp​≥W1​ (§3) and, for every coupling, ∥E[X−Y]∥≤E∥X−Y∥.

Solution

Upper bound. With X∼α, the pair (X,X+v) is a coupling of α and τv​#​α, of cost E∥v∥p=∥v∥p. So Wp​≤∥v∥.

Lower bound. For any coupling (X,Y) of the two measures, E[Y]−E[X]=v (the means differ by v), so ∥v∥=∥E[Y−X]∥≤E∥Y−X∥ (triangle inequality for integrals). Minimising over couplings: ∥v∥≤W1​≤Wp​. Hence Wp​=∥v∥: translating a distribution moves it, in Wasserstein distance, by exactly the length of the translation — whatever its shape.

Exercise 3 — The mechanics of gluing ★★

Let α=31​(δ0​+δ1​+δ2​), β=21​(δ0​+δ2​), γ=21​(δ0​+δ2​) on R, with the plans

P=​1/31/60​01/61/3​​∈U(α,β),Q=(1/41/4​1/41/4​)∈U(β,γ).

Compute the glued tensor S and the glued plan R∈U(α,γ). What do you notice? Is Q optimal?

Hint

Compute Qjk​/bj​ first: it is the same for all j,k.

Solution

b=(21​,21​) and Qjk​/bj​=1/21/4​=21​ for all j,k. So Sijk​=21​Pij​ and Rik​=∑j​Sijk​=21​∑j​Pij​=21​ai​=61​ for all i,k: R=ac⊤ is the independent plan. Gluing with an independent second plan forgets everything about the first one: “Z is independent of Y, hence of X”. Q is not optimal (the diagonal plan diag(21​,21​) costs 0, since β=γ); the gluing construction works with any plans, but the triangle inequality only follows when they are optimal.

Exercise 4 — For W1​, the mixture is a geodesic ★

Let mt​=(1−t)δx​+tδy​ on R with x=y. Compute W1​(ms​,mt​) and W2​(ms​,mt​) for s≤t. Is t↦mt​ a constant-speed geodesic for W1​? For W2​?

Hint

Keep the common part in place; how much mass must move, and how far?

Solution

The mass t−s must move from x to y, everything else stays: W1​(ms​,mt​)=(t−s)∣x−y∣ and W2​(ms​,mt​)=t−s​∣x−y∣. For W1​: W1​(ms​,mt​)=(t−s)W1​(m0​,m1​), the definition of a constant-speed geodesic: yes. For W2​: no — t−s​=t−s, and the path has infinite length (§6). Geodesics of W1​ are not unique (the displacement δ(1−t)x+ty​ is another one); this is one reason why W2​ is preferred for interpolation.

Exercise 5 — Two geodesics between the same two measures ★★

In R2, let α=21​(δ(−1,0)​+δ(1,0)​) and β=21​(δ(0,−2)​+δ(0,2)​). Find all optimal plans for W2​, and the corresponding displacement interpolations at t=21​.

Hint

Compute the four squared distances between the points of α and of β.

Solution

All four squared distances equal 1+4=5, so every coupling costs 5: all couplings are optimal and W22​=5. With rows (−1,0),(1,0) and columns (0,−2),(0,2), the couplings are Ps​=(s21​−s​21​−ss​), s∈[0,21​]: infinitely many optimal plans, and as many geodesics. At t=21​,

α1/2​=s(δ(−21​,−1)​+δ(21​,1)​)+(21​−s)(δ(−21​,1)​+δ(21​,−1)​).

The two pairings (s=21​ and s=0) give two-atom midpoints; the independent plan (s=41​) gives the uniform law on the four points (±21​,±1). Geodesics in the Wasserstein space need not be unique when the optimal plan is not (here, no density). Compare with §7: same phenomenon for barycenters.

Exercise 6 — The comparison of §3 is sharp for every pair p≤q ★★

On X=[0,1], let α=δ0​ and β=(1−ε)δ0​+εδ1​. Show that Wq​(α,β)=Wp​(α,β)p/q for all 1≤p≤q. Deduce that no inequality Wq​≤CWpr​ with r>p/q can hold on [0,1].

Solution

Wp​=ε1/p, so Wpp/q​=ε1/q=Wq​: equality in the right inequality (with diam=1). If Wq​≤CWpr​ held with r>p/q, then ε1/q≤Cεr/p, i.e. ε1/q−r/p≤C for all small ε; but q1​−pr​<0, so the left side blows up as ε→0. Contradiction.

Exercise 7 — Shifting a density versus shifting a Dirac ★★

Compute ∥N(0,1)−N(ε,1)∥TV​ and W1​(N(0,1),N(ε,1)), and compare with δ0​ versus δε​.

Hint

The two densities cross at x=ε/2. Write Φ for the standard Gaussian CDF.

Solution

For x<ε/2 the first density is larger, after it the second one. So ∥⋅∥TV​=2∫−∞ε/2​(φ(x)−φ(x−ε))dx=2(Φ(2ε​)−Φ(−2ε​))=2(2Φ(2ε​)−1)≈2εφ(0)≈0.80ε (for ε=0.1: 0.0798). By Exercise 2, W1​=ε. Both go to 0 linearly: for smooth densities, small shifts are small in TV too. For Diracs, ∥δ0​−δε​∥TV​=2 while W1​=ε: the difference between the two topologies comes from singular (atomic) measures.

Exercise 8 — Moments through W2​ ★

Show that W2​(α,δ0​)2=E∥X∥2 for X∼α, and deduce ​E∥X∥2​−E∥Y∥2​​≤W2​(α,β) for X∼α, Y∼β.

Solution

The only coupling of α with δ0​ sends x to 0: W22​(α,δ0​)=∫∥x∥2dα. The reverse triangle inequality for the distance W2​ gives ∣W2​(α,δ0​)−W2​(β,δ0​)∣≤W2​(α,β). This is the argument of §4 that Wp​-convergence implies convergence of the p-th moments.

Exercise 9 — Gaussian barycenter with commuting covariances ★★

Compute the W2​ barycenter of N(0,diag(1,4)) and N(0,diag(9,1)) with weights λ=(41​,43​), and check the fixed-point equation Ψ(Σ⋆)=Σ⋆.

Hint

For diagonal matrices everything happens coordinate by coordinate, as in 1D: average the standard deviations.

Solution

Coordinate 1: standard deviations 1 and 3, average 41​+49​=2.5. Coordinate 2: 2 and 1, average 21​+43​=1.25. So Σ⋆=diag(6.25, 1.5625) and the barycenter is N(0,Σ⋆). Check: for commuting matrices (Σ1/2Σk​Σ1/2)1/2=Σ1/2Σk1/2​, so Ψ(Σ⋆)=Σ⋆1/2(41​Σ11/2​+43​Σ21/2​)=diag(2.5,1.25)diag(2.5,1.25)=Σ⋆. ✓ (Also checked numerically with the general iteration.)

Exercise 10 — The commuting case in general ★★★

Assume that Σ1​,…,ΣP​ are positive definite and commute. Show that Σ⋆=(∑k​λk​Σk1/2​)2 satisfies Ψ(Σ⋆)=Σ⋆, hence is the barycenter covariance.

Hint

Commuting symmetric matrices can be diagonalised in a common orthonormal basis; then all square roots are taken eigenvalue by eigenvalue.

Solution

Write Σk​=UDk​U⊤ with a common orthogonal U and diagonal Dk​>0. Then S:=∑k​λk​Σk1/2​=U(∑k​λk​Dk1/2​)U⊤ and Σ⋆=S2, so (Σ⋆)1/2=S, which commutes with every Σk​. Hence (Σ⋆1/2Σk​Σ⋆1/2)1/2=(S2Σk​)1/2=SΣk1/2​ (all diagonal in the basis U, with positive entries). Therefore Ψ(Σ⋆)=∑k​λk​SΣk1/2​=S⋅S=Σ⋆. By the board’s proposition (uniqueness of the positive definite fixed point), Σ⋆ is the barycenter covariance.

Exercise 11 — A 1D barycenter by quantiles ★★

Compute the W2​ barycenter of β1​=U[0,2]​ and β2​=21​(δ0​+δ2​) with weights 21​,21​. Draw it.

Hint

Cβ1​−1​(t)=2t; Cβ2​−1​(t)=0 for t≤21​ and 2 for t>21​.

Solution

The average quantile function is t for t≤21​ and t+1 for t>21​. It increases with slope 1 on two intervals of t of length 21​, with a jump in between: the barycenter is the uniform density 1 on [0,21​]∪[23​,2] (two blocks of mass 21​). The Dirac at 0 “pulls” the left half of the uniform halfway towards it and shrinks it by half; the same on the right. A mixture would have given the uniform plus two atoms.

Exercise 12 — One run of the fixed-point algorithm by hand ★★★

In R2, with weights 21​,21​: β1​=21​(δ(0,1)​+δ(1,1)​), β2​=21​(δ(0,−1)​+δ(2,−1)​), and the starting guess α(0)=21​(δ(0,0)​+δ(1,0)​). Run the point-cloud version of the algorithm (§9) until it stops. Check the descent inequality, and show that the result is the true barycenter.

Hint

For each input, compare the two possible assignments. For the last question, use the lower bound t(1−t)W22​(β1​,β2​) of §6.

Solution

Step 1. To β1​: (0,0)→(0,1) and (1,0)→(1,1) (cost 1+1, against 2+2 for the crossed assignment). To β2​: (0,0)→(0,−1) and (1,0)→(2,−1) (cost 1+2, against 5+2). Averaging the partners: (0,0)↦(0,0), (1,0)↦21​(1,1)+21​(2,−1)=(1.5,0). So α(1)=21​(δ(0,0)​+δ(1.5,0)​).

Costs. F(α(0))=21​⋅1+21​⋅1.5=1.25; F(α(1))=21​⋅1.125+21​⋅1.125=1.125; squared step length 21​⋅0.52=0.125. Descent: 1.125≤1.25−0.125 (equality here). ✓

Step 2. The assignments do not change, and the averages are again (0,0) and (1.5,0): fixed point, the algorithm stops.

Optimality. Between β1​ and β2​ the optimal plan pairs (0,1)↔(0,−1) (cost 4) and (1,1)↔(2,−1) (cost 5): W22​(β1​,β2​)=4.5. By §6, every candidate has F≥21​⋅21​⋅4.5=1.125. α(1) attains it, so it is a barycenter (it is the midpoint of the geodesic).

Exercise 13 — Barycenters for W1​ are very non-unique ★★

On R, find all the minimisers of α↦21​W1​(α,δ0​)+21​W1​(α,δ1​).

Solution

By the Dirac computation of §7 the objective is ∫Fdα with F(x)=21​∣x∣+21​∣x−1∣. F=21​ on [0,1] and F>21​ outside. So the minimisers are all probability measures carried by [0,1]: δ1/2​, the mixture 21​(δ0​+δ1​), U[0,1]​, … The quadratic cost (W22​) selects a unique answer, δ1/2​. This is the median-versus-mean phenomenon of §7, lifted to distributions.

11. Summary of the lecture#

The lecture on one screen
  1. Kantorovich (§1): Lc​(α,β)=minπ∈U(α,β)​∫cdπ=minX∼α,Y∼β​E[c(X,Y)]; for ∥x−y∥2 and α with a density, the optimal plan is a map T=∇φ (Brenier).
  2. Wp​ is a distance (§2): Wp​=Ldp1/p​, p≥1. Symmetry and positivity from d; Wp​=0⇒ an optimal coupling with X=Y a.s. ⇒α=β; triangle inequality by gluing Sijk​=παβ​(i,j)πβγ​(j,k)/bj​, then triangle inequality of d, then Minkowski.
  3. Comparison (§3): on a compact space, Wp​≤Wq​≤diamqq−p​Wpp/q​ (p≤q). Same convergent sequences, different values and rates (W1​=ε, W2​=ε​).
  4. Weak convergence (§4): test against Cb​ (weak), C0​ (weak-*), Cc​ (vague); equivalent for probability limits; one notion on compact spaces. Wp​ metrizes it on compact spaces; on Rd, Wp​-convergence = weak + convergence of p-th moments (escaping mass).
  5. Total variation (§5): ∥α−β∥TV​=sup∥f∥∞​≤1​∫fd(α−β) = total mass that differs; for the 0/1 distance, Wpp​=21​∥α−β∥TV​. Diracs and Riemann sums never converge in TV (=2), they do in Wp​; on finite spaces the two topologies coincide.
  6. Geodesics (§6): αt​=Pt​#​π, Pt​(x,y)=(1−t)x+ty, moves mass along straight lines; W2​(αs​,αt​)=∣t−s∣W2​(α,β); (P2​(Rd),W2​) is a geodesic space; the mixture is not a geodesic. αt​ minimises (1−t)W22​(α,ρ)+tW22​(β,ρ).
  7. Barycenters (§7): minα​∑k​λk​Lc​(α,βk​), the Fréchet mean of distributions. Diracs → Dirac at the mean; fixed grid → LP; on Rd with W2​: exists, unique if one input with positive weight has a density (Agueh–Carlier).
  8. Closed forms (§8): Gaussians → N(∑λk​mk​,Σ⋆) with Σ⋆=Ψ(Σ⋆), Ψ(Σ)=∑k​λk​(Σ1/2Σk​Σ1/2)1/2; 1D → Cα−1​=∑k​λk​Cβk​−1​ (average quantiles).
  9. Algorithm (§9): α(ℓ+1)=(∑k​λk​Tk​)#​α(ℓ); it decreases the cost by at least W22​(α(ℓ),α(ℓ+1)); barycenters satisfy ∑k​λk​Tk​=Id. Exact in one step in 1D; on Gaussians it is the Álvarez-Esteban covariance update.

The reflexes to acquire#

  • Upper bound on a transport cost → exhibit one coupling.
  • Coupling of α and γ from couplings through β → glue (conditionally independent given the middle).
  • Any new claim about Wp​ → test it on Diracs first.
  • p≥1 and a p-th root → Minkowski. A power sr, r≥1, of an average → Jensen.
  • Two transport costs with comparable ground costs → compare the integrands under a good coupling.
  • “αn​→α” → against which test functions? On Rd, check the moments (escaping mass).
  • Total variation → “mass that differs”; it ignores distances; mutually singular measures are at distance 2.
  • Interpolate distributions → move positions along an optimal plan, do not mix weights.
  • Average distributions → barycenter = Fréchet mean; on the line, average quantiles; for Gaussians, means and covariances separate.
  • Barycenter condition → the average of the optimal maps from the barycenter is the identity.

What comes next#

  • Lesson 4 (duality). The dual of the Kantorovich problem, c-transforms (Exercise 3 of the sheet), and the Kantorovich–Rubinstein formula W1​=supLip(f)≤1​∫fd(α−β), which completes the proof that Wp​ metrizes weak convergence (§4).
  • Lesson 6 (dynamic OT). The geodesics of §6 become curves of minimal kinetic energy (Benamou–Brenier), the starting point of flow matching.
  • Lesson 7 (entropic regularization). Fast approximate barycenters on grids (Sinkhorn barycenters), the practical answer to the size of the LP of §7.
  • Lesson 8 (gradient flows). Moving in the Wasserstein space along its geometry; the barycenter algorithm of §9 is already a gradient descent there.

Notes on the sources (things that could confuse you)
  • Exponent in the comparison of the Wp​. CourseOT.pdf, Prop. 8, prints Wpq/p​; the correct exponent is p/q, as in your notes (§3).
  • Factor 21​ for the 0/1 cost. Peyré–Cuturi, Remark 2.26, states LC​(a,b)=∥a−b∥1​; the correct value is 21​∥a−b∥1​, as on the board (§5). Some books call 21​∥α−β∥TV​ “the total variation distance”: check the convention.
  • “To check” on the board. ∥δxn​​−δx​∥TV​=2 for xn​=x: checked three ways in §5.
  • The Gaussian iteration. The board’s Σ←Ψ(Σ) converges in practice (Peyré–Cuturi, Remark 9.5; and in all our tests) but no general proof is given there; the Álvarez-Esteban update Σ←Σ−1/2Ψ(Σ)2Σ−1/2 is proved to converge and is what the general algorithm of the board does on Gaussians (§8–§9).
  • Agueh–Carlier “2010”. The paper appeared in 2011 (SIAM J. Math. Anal.); 2010 is the preprint.
  • Two meanings of P1​. In §1, P1​,P2​ are the first and second projections; in §6, P0​,P1​ are the endpoints of Pt​ (time 0 and 1). Same letters, different indexing.
  • Two meanings of γ. A third measure in the triangle inequality (§2), a path in the definition of a geodesic space (§6).
  • Other letters with two meanings on the board. P: the number of inputs, and the plans Pk​ of the LP (§7). B(x1​,…,xP​): the barycenter (§7); B: the Bures distance (§8). φ: a test function (§4), a convex potential (Brenier), Jensen’s convex function (§3). c: the cost, and ck​ the weights of γ (§2). f: a test function, and the density of α−β in the TV example (§5).
  • Two small slips in the notes, corrected on this page. In the comparison of the Wp​ (§3) the powers q are missing on Wp​ and Wq​ in the Jensen line; the uniqueness of the Gaussian fixed point (§8) holds among positive definite matrices (Ψ(0)=0).
